bill_summary: This bill increases the maximum annual revenue limit for a cottage food business from $50,000 to $100,000, allowing more small-scale food producers to operate from residential kitchens without a food manufacturing license.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Cottage food business owners, residential food producers, the Maryland Department of Health, local health departments, and consumers of cottage food products.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures increase by $52,400 in FY 2027 for the Maryland Department of Health to hire a part-time registered sanitarian to manage increased cottage food business registrations and inquiries. These costs are projected to rise to approximately $67,700 by FY 2031. General fund revenues may see a minimal, indeterminate decrease if businesses choose to operate as cottage food businesses rather than paying for food manufacturing licenses. Local health departments can likely manage any associated increase in workload with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary regulatory agency for cottage food businesses. The bill amends the Health - General Article, and the fiscal note indicates MDH will require additional staff and funding to manage an increase in requests for unique identification numbers, label reviews, and food safety certifications resulting from the increased revenue cap.

The Department of Agriculture supports the marketing of local agricultural products and the viability of farming. Since cottage food products are frequently sold at farmer's markets, and the agency was consulted in the fiscal analysis, this bill impacts the micro-businesses within the agricultural ecosystem they support.

The bill has a direct fiscal impact on the state's general fund, specifically requiring the creation of a new part-time registered sanitarian position. DBM is responsible for supervising budget execution and managing state personnel resources.

The bill doubles the annual revenue threshold for cottage food businesses, which acts as an economic stimulus for small, home-based entrepreneurs by allowing them to expand operations before being subject to more stringent commercial licensing requirements.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the Department of Health and is responsible for signing the bill into law and ensuring its implementation aligns with broader state policy priorities regarding small business and public health.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland Department of Health and will be involved in advising the agency on regulatory updates needed to comply with the new statutory definition of a cottage food business.

As the state's chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller monitors business revenues. The shift of businesses from licensed manufacturers to cottage food businesses may impact tax reporting and revenue streams overseen by this agency.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland State Department of Education to make a professional development course on educator well-being and flourishing available to all school personnel and administrators by July 1, 2027. stakeholders: Maryland school personnel and administrators
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures are not expected to be materially affected as the Maryland State Department of Education can fulfill the bill's requirements using existing resources, such as a course currently provided by Georgetown University. Furthermore, the department is only required to offer the course if it can be done at no cost or at a cost comparable to similar professional development courses. Local school system finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the State Department of Education (MSDE) to develop or provide a professional development course on educator well-being and flourishing for all school personnel and administrators.

As an independent unit within MSDE responsible for providing training and fostering supportive learning environments, this agency may be involved in delivering the well-being and flourishing curriculum, particularly regarding the 'feeling safe' component of the environmental well-being dimension.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and MSDE. The Governor must approve the bill, and the office coordinates the policy initiatives and budget proposals that would encompass this educational requirement.

DBM is responsible for supervising budget execution and estimating revenues. While the fiscal note suggests no material impact, the agency monitors the general fund expenditures of MSDE related to program implementation.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MSDE and would likely review any third-party contracts or licenses required to adapt or make available the professional development course specified in the bill.

The MLDS Center links student and workforce data, including educator performance and professional development outcomes. The tracking of completion of this professional development course may eventually integrate into their data collection.

The PERB oversees collective bargaining for public school personnel. Changes to professional development requirements or availability can sometimes intersect with labor-management relations and working conditions for school staff.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Secretary of Agriculture to submit an annual report identifying additional agricultural equipment that should qualify for an income tax subtraction modification. Additionally, the bill establishes a $1,000 refundable income tax credit for parents who experience a stillbirth, with the credit amount phasing out for individuals with a federal adjusted gross income over $100,000 and for joint filers over $150,000.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Agriculture and the Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Maryland agricultural producers (farmers) and parents of stillborn children.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the Maryland Department of Agriculture can implement the bill's reporting requirements with existing budgeted resources and State revenues are not affected. However, the bill text also creates a $1,000 refundable income tax credit for parents of stillborn children for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2026, which would likely result in a future reduction of State income tax revenue not reflected in the provided Fiscal Note's specific figures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the primary agency responsible for administering the state's tax laws. This bill creates a new refundable income tax credit for parents of stillborn children and modifies an existing subtraction modification for agricultural equipment, both of which require the Comptroller to update tax forms, process claims, and manage the resulting revenue impacts.

The bill mandates that the Secretary of Agriculture report annually to the Governor and General Assembly with recommendations for new equipment to qualify for tax subtractions. Furthermore, the agency is responsible for certifying that taxpayers are in compliance with requirements to receive these tax modifications.

The bill's new $1,000 tax credit is contingent upon the issuance of a 'Certificate of Birth Resulting in Stillbirth' under the Health – General Article. The Department of Health oversees the Vital Statistics Administration, which handles the issuance of such certificates.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and budget supervision. The implementation of a new refundable tax credit and expanded subtraction modifications will affect the state's general fund revenues, requiring DBM's oversight.

The Secretary of Agriculture is required by the bill to submit an annual report specifically to the Governor regarding recommended agricultural equipment for tax modifications. Additionally, the Governor oversees the executive agencies implementing the bill's provisions.

The Maryland Tax Court hears appeals regarding final decisions made by taxing authorities. Disputed claims for the new stillborn child credit or the agricultural equipment subtraction would eventually be adjudicated by this court.

bill_summary: The Maryland Housing Certainty Act mandates that local regulatory authorities and the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission review housing development applications based on the laws and regulations in effect when a complete application is submitted. The bill grants developers vested rights to authorized use and development for at least five years after approval and prohibits the collection of development impact fees or excise taxes until construction is complete and occupancy permits are issued, with exceptions for certain pre-existing county debt.
responsible_party: Local regulatory authorities and the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission (M-NCPPC)
stakeholders: Residential housing developers, construction small businesses, local government planning and zoning departments, and the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not directly affected. Local government expenditures may increase to manage new administrative requirements for tracking application completeness and vesting periods. Local revenues from development impact fees and excise taxes will be delayed until construction completion; while specific loss estimates are unavailable, the aggregate annual revenue from these sources across Maryland counties was approximately 179,217,515 for fiscal 2025. This delay may necessitate increased local borrowing or delayed infrastructure spending.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy and proposed this legislation as part of a housing policy agenda. The bill focuses on housing certainty and economic mobility, which are key executive priorities.

The OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to state agencies regarding the implementation of the new 'vested rights' statutory framework, which replaces existing common law standards established by the courts.

The bill impacts the business climate for the housing and development industries by providing regulatory certainty and delaying fee collection, which aligns with the agency's mission to stimulate the economy and attract business.

The bill delays the collection of local development impact fees, which are a primary source of funding for local school systems and infrastructure. This delay impacts the timing of revenue for educational facilities.

The bill mandates that permit approvals be governed by laws in effect at the time of application. This potentially affects environmental permits related to housing projects that MDE oversees or coordinates with local jurisdictions.

As the state's primary housing agency, DHCD is directly involved in policy related to residential real estate projects, housing expansion, and the economic vitality of Maryland communities affected by this bill.

MDP is the primary agency for state land use policy and providing guidance to local jurisdictions on planning and zoning. This bill makes significant amendments to the Land Use Article and local permitting procedures, which MDP oversees.
Local development impact fees and excise taxes often fund transportation infrastructure. Delaying these fees affects the funding timeline for roads and transit projects that support new developments.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The regulatory certainty and delayed fee collection provided by the bill may benefit small, minority, and women-owned businesses operating in the residential construction and development sectors.
The bill establishes new statutory 'vested rights' for property use, which will likely lead to increased litigation and requires the judiciary to interpret new legal standards for land use disputes.

The IAC manages funding for school construction projects. The bill's delay of impact fee collection directly impacts the revenue streams that local jurisdictions use to fund the school projects overseen by the IAC.

MEDCO provides financing and real estate development services. Changes in permitting laws and fee collection timing affect the feasibility and financing models of development projects supported by the agency.

The MSA manages the construction of public schools through the Built to Learn Act. The delay in local impact fee collection impacts the overall funding environment for the school facility improvements the MSA executes.

The team is tasked with addressing the Governor's top priorities, including enhancing economic mobility and reducing poverty. Improving housing certainty is a core component of this economic strategy.

The Tax Court adjudicates disputes regarding local taxes, including excise taxes. The bill's new restrictions on the collection of development excise taxes may lead to administrative appeals within this court's jurisdiction.
The bill's impact on land use planning and developer fees affects the economic development and infrastructure funding models of Maryland's 18 rural counties.

This multi-agency initiative is grounded in the land use planning visions that this bill amends. It coordinates sustainable development policy across departments, making it highly relevant to the bill's permitting reforms.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Commission on the House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children to investigate the historical operations, resident deaths, and unmarked graves at the former reformatory institution. The commission is tasked with identifying the deceased through archaeological and DNA analysis, notifying descendants, and recommending systemic reforms, reparations, and a permanent memorial.
responsible_party: Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Descendants of children buried at the site, former residents of the institution, African American communities in Maryland, and state agencies such as the Department of Juvenile Services and the Maryland Historical Trust.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $1,050,000 in FY 2027, reflecting funding included in the FY 2027 budget. Additional indeterminate expenditure increases may occur in FY 2028 and FY 2029 to support the commission's work. The Office of the Attorney General is expected to staff the commission using existing resources. Local government finances are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Attorney General chairs the commission, and the office is responsible for providing staff, administering funding, making public member appointments, procuring services, and exercising subpoena power for the investigation.

The Secretary of Juvenile Services is a member of the commission. The department operates the successor facility (Cheltenham Youth Detention Center) and its records and facilities are primary subjects of the commission's investigation.

The Director of the Maryland Historical Trust, which resides within this department, is a member of the commission. The commission must also consult with the Trust on archaeological methods and safety regarding the disinterment of human remains.
The State Archivist is a member of the commission, and the agency's records are a primary source for the historical research and identification of children buried at the site.
The commission is required to consult with the department regarding safety methods for disinterment and is granted access to the department's medical and administrative records for the investigation.
The Chief Archaeologist of the State Highway Administration is specifically named as a member of the commission, providing technical expertise for the archaeological surveys.

The State Superintendent of Schools is a member of the commission. Additionally, the commission is tasked with recommending educational initiatives to incorporate the history of the institution into the state's curriculum.
The Secretary of Human Services is a member of the commission, reflecting the department's role in oversight of children's welfare and historical state care.
The Secretary of General Services is a member of the commission, likely due to the agency's role in managing state-owned facilities and grounds where the cemetery is located.
The Secretary of Veterans and Military Families is a member of the commission and is involved in developing the cemetery conservation plan.

As the parent agency of the State Highway Administration, the department's Chief Archaeologist is a member of the commission, and the agency is mentioned in the fiscal note regarding the investigation.
The commission is required to submit both initial and final reports of its findings and recommendations to the Governor.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the state budget which provides the funding for the commission's operations and contracted research.
The bill bypasses certain confidentiality statutes related to court records, granting the commission access to sealed juvenile records held by the Judiciary.
A representative from the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law is a member of the commission, and USM institutions are prioritized for procurement of research services.
As a prominent Historically Black College and University (HBCU) in Maryland, the university is a preferred institution for the procurement of goods and services required by the commission.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill establishes a new state commission to conduct a specific, time-limited historical and forensic investigation.

Synopsis: Requiring the Commissioner of Labor and Industry to post a user-friendly, searchable database of active elevator inspection certificates on the Maryland Department of Labor's website; and requiring the database to be searchable by street address, city, and county.
Title: Public Safety - Elevator Inspection Certificates - Searchable Database
bill_summary: This bill requires the Commissioner of Labor and Industry to post a user-friendly, searchable database of active elevator inspection certificates on the Maryland Department of Labor's website. The database must permit users to search for certificates by street address, city, and county.
responsible_party: Commissioner of Labor and Industry, Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Elevator owners and lessees, the general public, and the Maryland Department of Labor
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Labor can likely implement the bill with existing resources. However, if current online resources (such as an Excel spreadsheet) do not meet the user-friendly database requirement, general fund expenditures may increase by a one-time cost of $75,000 to add a module to the existing internal database. There is no impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Commissioner of Labor and Industry, an official within the Maryland Department of Labor, to create and maintain the searchable elevator inspection certificate database on the department's website. The department is the primary agency responsible for enforcing the public safety laws related to elevator inspections.

As the agency responsible for the state's information technology strategy and digital services, the Department of Information Technology may provide technical oversight, support, or implementation services for the creation of the user-friendly searchable database module required on the state's website.

The fiscal note indicates a potential one-time general fund expenditure of $75,000 to implement the database module if existing resources are insufficient. DBM oversees state budget execution and fiscal planning related to these expenditures.

It also alters the membership of the Legislative Policy Committee by adding the chair of the House Government, Labor, and Elections Committee and adjusting the number of other appointed delegates.

stakeholders: Members of the Maryland General Assembly, legislative standing committees, and State agencies required to submit reports to the legislature
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is technical in nature and has no effect on State or local governmental operations or finances, with no revenue or expenditure changes reported in the fiscal note.

The bill updates the legislative reporting requirements for the Commissioner of Labor and Industry (within the Department) regarding modifications or directives related to the federal Bloodborne Pathogen Standard.
The bill updates the names of the legislative committees to which the Exchange's Board must submit proposed regulations and plans for alternative contracting options or active purchasing strategies.

The bill explicitly names the State Archivist and updates the legislative committee chairs who may request the Archivist to review, evaluate, and make recommendations regarding official State designations.

The bill updates the reporting structure for several executive branch programs where the Governor is a co-recipient of reports alongside legislative committees, and it alters the membership of the Legislative Policy Committee which coordinates state policy.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a predetermination review process allowing individuals to request that certain state departments review their criminal history to determine if it would disqualify them from obtaining a specific occupational license or certificate before they apply. The process applies to the departments of Agriculture, Environment, Health, Human Services, and Labor, and departments are authorized to charge a fee of up to $100 for this service, which may be waived based on income level.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Agriculture, Maryland Department of the Environment, Maryland Department of Health, Department of Human Services, and Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Individuals with criminal records seeking occupational licenses or certificates and the state agencies responsible for professional licensing.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures increase by $50,800 in FY 2027 for the Maryland Department of Labor and the Maryland Department of Agriculture to manage administrative functions and one-time computer programming costs. Expenditures are estimated at $22,500 in FY 2028 and $23,500 in FY 2029 before the bill's termination. Revenue impact is indeterminate but expected to be minimal, as the $100 maximum fee may be offset by administrative costs and required fee waivers for individuals with incomes at or below 300% of the federal poverty level.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive departments mandated to implement the predetermination review process and will receive reports on the implementation and costs of the program by October 2028.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the impacted departments regarding the interpretation and implementation of the new predetermination review process, particularly its binding nature.

The Department of Agriculture is one of the five primary departments required to establish a predetermination review process and report on its implementation. The fiscal note identifies specific IT programming costs for this agency.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for the state's personnel and budget execution; it will oversee the funding for new contractual positions and IT upgrades necessitated by the bill at the departments of Labor and Agriculture.
The Department of the Environment is explicitly named as a department required to implement the criminal history predetermination review process and submit progress reports to the General Assembly.

The Maryland Department of Health is a primary implementing agency for the predetermination process, managing a high volume of professional licensing boards that will be impacted by the new requirements.
The Department of Human Services is explicitly mandated by the bill to implement the predetermination review process for its occupational licenses and certificates.

The Department of Information Technology may be involved in supporting the computer programming and online application updates required by agencies like the Department of Agriculture to implement the review process.

The Department of Labor is a primary implementing agency and, according to the fiscal note, will require additional contractual staff to manage the administrative workload of the predetermination process due to its extensive licensing responsibilities.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly removes this department from the definition of entities prohibited from denying licenses solely based on criminal history under this section. Additionally, it manages the criminal history records that the other departments will review.
The Maryland State Police may be involved in providing or validating criminal history records used by the five departments during the predetermination review process.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office advises on criminal justice strategies and the rehabilitation of justice-involved individuals, which aligns with the bill's policy of removing barriers to employment for ex-offenders.
The board coordinates workforce solutions and paths to prosperity; removing licensing barriers for individuals with criminal records is a key component of state workforce participation strategy.

The bill specifies that the District Court of Maryland (part of the Judicial Branch supported by the AOC) is responsible for determining whether an individual's income qualifies them for a fee waiver for the predetermination review.

The Commission enforces anti-discrimination laws in state contracts and employment; the bill's provisions regarding the use of criminal history in licensing decisions overlap with the Commission's oversight of fair practices.
As a regulatory unit within the Maryland Department of Health, the Commission is subject to the bill's requirements for units within the primary departments to implement predetermination reviews.
The OAH adjudicates contested cases from state agencies; denials of licenses or certifications following a predetermination review could result in appeals that are heard by Administrative Law Judges.
This agency is a division of the Maryland Department of Health that issues CDS permits, making it a licensing unit that must comply with the bill's predetermination review mandates.

Synopsis: Repealing the restriction on the number of wine festival licenses that the Board of License Commissioners for Prince George's County may issue annually; and repealing a prohibition on issuing a wine festival license for use in the 24th legislative district.
Title: Prince George's County - Alcoholic Beverages - Wine Festival Licenses PG 316-26
bill_summary: This bill renames the Prince George’s County Wine Festival license to the wine festival license and authorizes the Prince George’s County Board of License Commissioners to issue multiple wine festival licenses annually, repealing the previous limit of one license per year. It also removes the prohibition against issuing a wine festival license in the 24th legislative district.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Prince George’s County
stakeholders: Retail alcoholic beverages license holders, Class 3 winery license holders, Class 4 limited winery license holders, and residents of the 24th legislative district in Prince George's County.
fiscal_impact_summary: There is no State fiscal impact. Locally, the bill does not materially affect Prince George’s County operations or finances. Prince George's County anticipates a negligible revenue increase of approximately $225 annually, calculated from the issuance of up to three additional wine festival licenses at a fee of $75 each.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is explicitly tasked with regulating the alcohol industry in Maryland. This bill modifies licensing provisions for wine festivals in Prince George's County, which falls under the broader scope of alcohol regulation.

The bill mandates that the Board of License Commissioners ensure the primary focus of wine festivals is the promotion of Maryland wine. This aligns with the Department of Agriculture's mission to promote the economic viability of agribusiness and the marketing of local agricultural products.

The Department of Commerce oversees tourism and economic development. Wine festivals serve as economic activities and attractions that contribute to the state's competitive position and the growth of the beverage industry.

Wine festivals are recreational and cultural attractions that stimulate the tourism economy. The bill's expansion of the number of festivals in Prince George's County provides additional opportunities for tourism promotion and destination marketing.

bill_summary: This bill mandates specific annual funding of $5,687,000 for the Maryland Child Care Credential Program for fiscal years 2028 through 2030, supporting achievement bonuses, training reimbursements, and training vouchers for child care providers.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE), Office of Child Care (OCC)
stakeholders: Child care staff and administrators, and small business child care providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $5,687,000 annually from fiscal 2028 through 2030 due to the reestablishment of mandated funding for the Maryland Child Care Credential Program. While the program has recently been funded through the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, that fund is projected to be exhausted by fiscal 2028, requiring general fund support. There is no fiscal impact on local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is the primary agency responsible for the oversight and leadership of the state's public education and child care systems. Its Office of Child Care (OCC) directly administers the Maryland Child Care Credential Program, awarding achievement bonuses, training reimbursements, and vouchers to child care providers.

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) is responsible for developing the state's budget and supervising budget execution. This bill reestablishes a mandated general fund appropriation of approximately $5.7 million per year from FY 2028 through FY 2030, which DBM must integrate into the state's long-term fiscal planning.

The Governor's Office is responsible for proposing the annual state budget and overseeing the executive branch. This bill specifically mandates that the Governor appropriate specific funding levels for the Maryland Child Care Credential Program in the annual budget bill for several fiscal years.

The Governor's Office for Children (GOC) coordinates statewide efforts to promote the well-being of children and families and reduce child poverty. Improving the credentials and retention of the child care workforce through this funding mandate directly aligns with GOC's mission to enhance support networks for families and children.

The Governor's Workforce Development Board (GWDB) is the governor's chief policy-making body for the state's workforce system. This bill's focus on professional development and credential attainment within the child care sector is a specific workforce development strategy that aligns with GWDB's goal of creating pathways to prosperity for Maryland workers.

The Maryland State Innovation Team is tasked with piloting initiatives to address the Governor's top priorities, specifically reducing child poverty. Because child care access and quality (supported by a credentialed workforce) are critical components of poverty reduction and economic mobility, this program is relevant to their data-driven policy focus.

bill_summary: This bill redefines and expands legal protections for animals used by law enforcement and search and rescue teams. It replaces the existing felony charge for harming a law enforcement animal with several misdemeanor charges for intentionally harassing, interfering with, injuring, or killing an 'emergency response animal,' which specifically includes dogs and horses. The bill also establishes specific penalties for these actions, including enhanced penalties if the acts occur during the commission of another crime, while providing legal defenses for necessity or protection against excessive force.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary, Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, and State and local law enforcement units
stakeholders: Law enforcement officers, search and rescue personnel, handlers of emergency response dogs and horses, and the general public.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not expected to materially affect State or local government finances. The reclassification of certain crimes from felonies to misdemeanors may shift some cases from circuit courts to the District Court, but the volume of such cases is historically low. No specific dollar estimates for revenue or expenditure changes were provided.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary statewide law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police utilizes K9 units and other animals in its operations. The bill directly protects these 'emergency response animals' and regulates the legal defenses available to individuals who may interfere with or harm them.

The bill's definition of 'emergency response animal' specifically includes search and rescue dogs and horses directed by a State agency to locate or rescue individuals, a function often coordinated or supported by MDEM.

The Maryland Natural Resources Police, a unit within DNR, utilizes K9s for law enforcement and search and rescue efforts in state parks and waterways, both of which are covered by the bill's expanded protections.
The bill repeals a felony and replaces it with several specific misdemeanors, which impacts court jurisdiction, caseloads, and the processing of criminal charges within the Maryland Judicial Branch.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The creation of new misdemeanor offenses and the modification of existing penalties for actions against emergency response animals will directly impact the caseload and defense strategies of public defenders representing indigent clients.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS utilizes K9 units for security within correctional facilities. Furthermore, the bill's changes to criminal penalties for animal cruelty and the potential for incarceration in state or local facilities affect the department's oversight of justice-involved individuals.
MDOT oversees the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) Police and the Transit Police, both of which utilize K9 units for security and law enforcement at toll facilities and transit hubs.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state law enforcement agencies and represents the state in criminal appeals, including those involving the newly established misdemeanor offenses.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP serves as the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies, and this bill modifies criminal law regarding the protection of law enforcement and emergency response assets.
The MDA oversees programs related to animal health and is the lead agency for general agricultural leadership, though its primary focus is not criminal law enforcement.
The Governor must sign the bill into law and oversees the executive branch departments (like MSP and MDEM) that employ these emergency response animals.

bill_summary: This bill, titled the Pet Cremation and Burial Services Consumer Protection Act, establishes regulatory requirements for providers of pet cremation and burial services. It mandates that providers distribute clear written descriptions of cremation types (private, partitioned, or communal) and provide certificates of authenticity to pet owners upon returning remains. Additionally, it requires providers to maintain detailed records for five years and designates violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, subject to specific civil and criminal penalties.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors
stakeholders: Pet owners, veterinarians, pet shops, funeral directors, and operators of pet cemeteries and crematories.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal impact on the State and local governments is expected to be minimal and absorbable within existing budgeted resources. While the bill establishes new criminal fines (up to $15,000 for a third offense) and civil penalties (up to $5,000), total State revenues are not expected to be materially affected. Small businesses providing pet cremation services may experience a meaningful impact due to new disclosure, recordkeeping, and procedural requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes new misdemeanor criminal penalties and allows the Attorney General to file civil actions in court for violations, which directly impacts the workload and administrative operations of the state court system.
The bill specifically requires registered cemeterians, cemetery operators, and licensees to distribute written descriptions of their pet cremation services to the Department of Agriculture.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the budgets of the Department of Health and Department of Labor, both of which will require existing or additional resources to enforce the bill's new regulatory requirements.

The bill establishes new consumer protection and disclosure requirements for pet cremation under the Health Occupations Article, which is overseen by the State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors, an entity within the Department of Health.
The bill establishes requirements for registered cemeterians and cemetery operators, who are currently regulated by the Office of Cemetery Oversight within the Department of Labor.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementing the bill (MDH, Labor, and Agriculture) and is responsible for the final approval and enactment of the legislation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates new misdemeanor offenses punishable by fines and imprisonment; the Office of the Public Defender is responsible for representing indigent individuals charged with these crimes.

OAH is responsible for adjudicating contested cases and disciplinary actions that may arise if the State Board of Morticians or the Office of Cemetery Oversight takes enforcement action against a licensee or registrant for violating the bill's provisions.

The bill categorizes violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act and explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to pursue civil enforcement, including seeking injunctions and civil penalties.

Synopsis: Authorizing the County Commissioners of Queen Anne's County to use revenue from development impact fees to finance the capital costs related to the replacement of public school facilities.

bill_summary: This bill expands the authorized uses of revenue from development impact fees in Queen Anne's County to include the financing of capital costs associated with replacing public school facilities.
responsible_party: County Commissioners of Queen Anne's County
stakeholders: Residents, students, and the public school system of Queen Anne's County
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, there is no state or local fiscal impact. The bill does not alter the amount of development impact fees collected or imposed by Queen Anne's County but instead expands the eligible uses for existing fee revenue to include school construction-related capital costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Interagency Commission on School Construction (IAC) is responsible for overseeing the planning and funding of public school construction and capital improvement projects. This bill directly concerns the local funding mechanisms for school facility replacement, and the fiscal note lists the IAC as an information source.

The fiscal note specifies that counties imposing development impact fees must annually report information regarding the collection and use of these fees to the Maryland Department of Planning (MDP). This bill expands the authorized uses of these fees in Queen Anne's County, which will be reflected in reports submitted to the MDP.

The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) provides leadership and oversight to public school systems. Since this bill provides a new local funding avenue for the replacement of public school facilities, it is relevant to the agency's mission regarding educational infrastructure.

The Rural Maryland Council (RMC) addresses challenges facing Maryland's rural counties, including Queen Anne's. The bill affects local infrastructure and economic development tools (impact fees) specifically within a rural jurisdiction.

This multi-agency initiative coordinates sustainable development and land-use planning. Development impact fees are a key planning tool used to mitigate the impacts of new construction, making the bill relevant to the initiative's oversight of infrastructure development.
The Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation passed by the General Assembly. This bill requires executive action to become law.
The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly, typically reviewing bills for legal sufficiency and constitutional compliance.

The Secretary of State is the custodian of official state records, including laws and executive orders. Once the bill is signed by the Governor, the Secretary of State will manage the recording of the new law.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "nonprofit housing corporation" for purposes of eligibility for an exemption from real property taxes and special assessments of the State or a political subdivision; exempting certain real property owned by certain subsidiary entities of a certain nonprofit housing corporation from taxes and special assessments of the State or a political subdivision; etc.

bill_summary: This bill redefines nonprofit housing corporation to include 501(c)(3) organizations focused on affordable housing and expands state and local property tax and special assessment exemptions to their subsidiary entities. It also defines affordable housing criteria based on federal tax credits or specific income and rent restrictions, while excluding certain properties in Baltimore City and projects that received prior local financial assistance.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Nonprofit housing corporations, subsidiary entities of nonprofit housing corporations, low-income households seeking affordable housing, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local property tax revenues will decrease by an indeterminate amount beginning in fiscal 2027. The specific financial impact depends on the number of nonprofit housing corporations and subsidiaries that qualify for the tax exemption under the bill's expanded definitions. State and local expenditures are not directly affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill directly amends the Housing and Community Development Article of the Maryland Code, specifically altering the definition and tax-exempt status of nonprofit housing corporations and their subsidiaries, which fall under the department's primary mission of fostering affordable housing.
As the state's chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller is directly impacted by changes to tax-exempt statuses and definitions that result in a decrease in State tax revenues.
The Treasurer manages state funds, including the Annuity Bond Fund which relies on property tax revenues for debt service. A decrease in property tax revenue affects state financial management.
DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. The bill's indeterminate impact on state property tax revenues requires the department to adjust fiscal projections.

The OAG would provide legal counsel to the Department of Housing and Community Development and other state entities regarding the interpretation and implementation of the revised definition of 'nonprofit housing corporation'.
The Governor oversees the executive branch and housing policy; this bill represents a notable shift in affordable housing policy and tax exemptions, which are key executive priorities.

This board hears appeals regarding property tax assessments and exemptions. Altering the eligibility for nonprofit housing corporations and their subsidiaries directly impacts the scope and criteria of their administrative reviews.
The Tax Court adjudicates appeals from taxing authorities. Changes to property tax exemptions for housing corporations may lead to factual and legal disputes that would be heard by this court.

The bill includes provisions that exempt real property of nonprofit housing corporations from certain judicial processes, such as levy and sale by virtue of an execution, which impacts court operations regarding judgment enforcement.

The Department of Planning promotes sustainable growth and land use; the expansion of affordable housing through tax incentives is a relevant component of state land use and community development policy.

The Innovation Team's mandate includes identifying strategies to reduce child poverty and enhance economic mobility, both of which are central goals of the affordable housing expansion addressed in this bill.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Department of Housing and Community Development to adopt certain regulations related to affirmatively furthering fair housing; providing that certain discriminatory housing practices may be committed without intent; prohibiting a person from acting in a certain manner that has a discriminatory effect; and providing that certain conduct necessary to achieve certain nondiscriminatory interests does not constitute a certain violation.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development to adopt regulations requiring political subdivisions and housing authorities to affirmatively further fair housing. It also prohibits housing practices that have a 'discriminatory effect' (disparate impact) regardless of intent, defining such effects as those that create or perpetuate segregated housing patterns, while establishing a defense for actions necessary to achieve legitimate, non-discriminatory interests where no less discriminatory alternative exists.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development, Maryland Commission on Civil Rights, and the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Maryland residents (specifically those in protected classes), local governments, housing authorities, landlords, and property owners.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances. It aligns Maryland law with the federal Fair Housing Act and judicial precedents regarding disparate impact theory in housing discrimination cases. Small business impacts are expected to be minimal as the bill codifies existing legal frameworks.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for enforcing Maryland's anti-discrimination laws in housing, MCCR is directly impacted by the bill's expansion of prohibited acts to include those with a 'discriminatory effect' regardless of intent.

The bill specifically authorizes this department to adopt regulations related to affirmatively furthering fair housing and mandates that it require political subdivisions and housing authorities to submit fair housing assessments.

The bill explicitly references the Attorney General's authority to investigate, prosecute, and remediate conduct that constitutes a civil rights violation, which includes the discriminatory housing acts defined in the bill.

This agency is responsible for conducting administrative hearings for housing discrimination claims brought through the Commission on Civil Rights, and the bill clarifies the legal standards for such cases.

The bill requires local jurisdictions to include fair housing assessments in the housing element of their comprehensive plans, a process that falls under the Department of Planning's technical assistance and land use oversight.
The bill provides for civil actions in State courts for alleged discriminatory housing practices, potentially impacting the judicial branch's caseload and legal interpretations of disparate impact.
Since disability is a primary protected class in fair housing law, this department is impacted as it advocates for the rights and community living accessibility of individuals with disabilities.
Military status is a protected class under the housing discrimination laws modified by this bill, making it relevant to the department's advocacy and support for military families.

bill_summary: This bill requires each Maryland county board of education to implement a student attendance policy that allows for excused or discretionary absences for students participating in civic engagement activities. These activities include testifying at legislative hearings, meeting with members of a legislative body, advocating for policy issues, and participating in the Maryland General Assembly Page Program. The policy must allow for at least 15 hours or two school days for these activities, and such absences cannot be factored into a student's chronic absenteeism calculation.
responsible_party: Maryland county boards of education
stakeholders: Public school students in Maryland and local school systems
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no financial impact on State or local government. According to the Fiscal Note, local school systems can modify their attendance policies and track civic engagement absences using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary oversight agency for Maryland's public education system, MSDE is responsible for state attendance policies and is specifically granted authority under the bill to deem certain activities as civic engagement for the purpose of excused absences.

This agency links and analyzes student performance and absenteeism data. The bill explicitly states that excused absences for civic engagement may not be included in calculations of chronic absenteeism, which directly impacts the agency's data reporting and analytical functions regarding student outcomes.

The Governor's Office for Children leads efforts to promote child well-being and access to educational opportunities. This bill supports youth development by facilitating student participation in the policy-making process, which aligns with the office's mission to improve opportunities for Maryland's children.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's definition of a 'legislative body' includes entities appointed by the Governor or local executives that are subject to the Open Meetings Act. Many executive commissions and task forces fall under this definition, serving as the venues where students would engage in the activities mentioned in the bill.

bill_summary: House Bill 578 updates Maryland's endangered and threatened species laws by defining 'foreseeable future' and 'harm,' authorizing the designation of 'essential habitats,' and requiring decennial and quinquennial reviews of conservation regulations. It also prohibits the taking of migratory birds protected under federal law as of January 1, 2025, while mandating state-level authorizations for taking black vultures if federal protections are repealed or removed.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Natural Resources
stakeholders: Maryland Department of Natural Resources, state and local government agencies, small businesses involved in land development, and the general public.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local expenditures may increase starting in fiscal 2027 to implement and enforce new habitat and migratory bird protections. The Department of Natural Resources expects additional resources will be required for permit reviews and enforcement, but the specific financial impact is currently indeterminate.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DNR is the primary agency responsible for implementing the bill, including managing the Irreplaceable Natural Areas Program, designating essential habitats, adopting management protocols, and promulgating regulations for endangered species and the taking of black vultures.

As noted in the fiscal note, the bill's strengthened protections for fish, wildlife, and migratory birds could impact the capital programs and infrastructure projects of MDOT's various administrations, such as SHA and MTA.

The bill explicitly requires the Secretary of DNR to consult with the Secretary of Agriculture regarding conservation programs. Additionally, the provisions regarding black vultures significantly impact the agricultural community.
DGS manages the planning, design, and construction of state-owned facilities; its capital projects may be impacted by the bill's new definitions for 'harm' and 'essential habitat' designations.
The OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to DNR regarding the new regulatory definitions of 'harm' and 'foreseeable future' and representing the agency in potential litigation.
MDP provides land use policy guidance and works with DNR on conservation initiatives. Essential habitat designations under the bill will intersect with the state's land use planning goals.
The BPW must approve the acquisition of land or interests in land for the conservation of threatened or endangered species, which is a program requirement under the bill.
The OAH would adjudicate contested cases resulting from DNR's enforcement of new regulations or the denial/granting of permits related to the taking of species or habitat modification.
As a state agency with significant capital construction programs across multiple institutions, USM was identified in the fiscal note as a potentially impacted entity.
The IAC oversees public school construction; projects could be affected by more stringent habitat and species protections established in the bill.
The MSA's construction activities, including professional sports venues and public schools, may be subject to the bill's new habitat and wildlife regulations.
This multi-agency initiative coordinates sustainable development and environmental protection, aligning directly with the bill's focus on biodiversity and habitat management.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Council advises on the restoration of the Bay watershed; the bill's habitat protections for endangered fish and wildlife are integral to these restoration efforts.
As a state agency with its own capital construction projects, MSU may be impacted by habitat and wildlife protections affecting urban campus development.
As an independent state unit with a waterfront campus, SMCM's construction or maintenance activities could be affected by new fish and habitat regulations.
DBM oversees DNR's budget and personnel, which the fiscal note indicates may need to increase to support the new regulatory and enforcement duties required by the bill.

Synopsis: Updating the name of a certain office from the County Department of Environmental Resources to the Department of Permitting, Inspections, and Enforcement to which the Board of License Commissioners for Prince George's County must provide notice when issuing a Class C per diem beer, wine, and liquor license.
Title: Prince George’s County – Alcoholic Beverages – Notice of Issuance of Class C Per Diem Beer, Wine, and Liquor License PG 319–26
bill_summary: This bill updates the name of the department that the Prince George's County Board of License Commissioners must notify when issuing a Class C per diem beer, wine, and liquor license. The notification recipient is changed from the Department of Environmental Resources to the Department of Permitting, Inspections, and Enforcement to reflect a previous county government restructuring.
responsible_party: Prince George's County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Prince George's County Board of License Commissioners, the Prince George's County Department of Permitting, Inspections, and Enforcement, and organizations applying for Class C per diem alcoholic beverages licenses in Prince George's County.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill has no state fiscal impact and does not materially affect Prince George's County operations or finances. The change is considered a technical update to reflect current department names.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the state's chief regulator of the alcohol industry. As this bill amends the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article regarding license notification procedures, it is relevant to the agency's oversight of state alcohol laws.

The Governor's Office is responsible for signing legislation into law and for appointing the members of the Prince George’s County Board of License Commissioners, the entity tasked with providing the notices described in the bill.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, boards, and commissions. The local Board of License Commissioners may require legal guidance from the OAG regarding its compliance with updated statutory notification requirements.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes county boards of library trustees to include a student member on their boards. It establishes the selection process, qualifications for high school juniors or seniors, a one-year term of office, and voting rights for the student member on policy and other board-authorized matters. Student members are required to be in good standing and serve without compensation.
responsible_party: County Boards of Library Trustees
stakeholders: High school juniors and seniors, county boards of library trustees, and county governing bodies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no State fiscal impact. Locally, the bill does not materially affect government finances or operations because board members serve without compensation and the selection of a student member is optional for each board.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Library is the primary state agency responsible for the strategic leadership and coordination of the 24 public library systems in Maryland. This bill directly alters the statutory membership structure of the county boards of library trustees that oversee these systems.

The bill authorizes the inclusion of student members on library boards, specifically high school students in public or nonpublic schools. As the oversight body for Maryland's public education system and the department responsible for student-related policies, MSDE is relevant to the selection and qualifications of these student members.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding statutory changes. As this bill amends the Education Article regarding the legal composition and voting rights of county boards, the OAG may be involved in providing legal guidance on implementation and governance.

Synopsis: Establishing the Workgroup on Transportation Contract Approval Authority to review the procurement procedures for capital expenditures in connection with State roads, bridges, or highways; and requiring the Workgroup to report its findings and recommendations to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2026.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Workgroup on Transportation Contract Approval Authority to review and evaluate the procurement procedures and approval structures for capital expenditures related to State roads, bridges, and highways. The workgroup is tasked with studying the justification for existing exemptions from Board of Public Works oversight, the potential effects of altering that structure, and the impact on project timelines and federal funding, with a final report due by December 1, 2026.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation and the Board of Public Works
stakeholders: Maryland Department of Transportation, Maryland Transportation Authority, Board of Public Works, engineering and design services industry, transportation construction and materials industry, Disadvantaged and Minority Business Enterprises, State labor organizations, and the Maryland Association of Counties.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note identifies no state or local financial impact. The Maryland Department of Transportation and the Board of Public Works are responsible for staffing the workgroup using existing resources, and any minimal expense reimbursements for workgroup members are expected to be absorbable within existing budgets.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Transportation (MDOT) is the primary subject of the bill. Its procurement procedures and capital expenditures are the focus of the study, the Secretary of Transportation is a member of the workgroup, and the department is tasked with jointly providing staff to support the workgroup's operations.

The Board of Public Works (BPW) is a central focus of the study, which evaluates whether its oversight should be expanded to include transportation capital contracts. Additionally, the BPW is mandated to jointly provide staffing for the workgroup.
The bill specifically mandates a study of the procurement procedures and capital expenditure approval structure of the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) for roads, bridges, and highways.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new temporary entity, the 'Workgroup on Transportation Contract Approval Authority', to conduct a study and provide recommendations, which falls under this collective agency designation.

The workgroup is explicitly required to evaluate whether current delegated procurement authority should be expanded to include maintenance and capital construction for Maryland Transit Administration (MTA) fixed guideway systems and associated facilities.

The Comptroller is a designated member of the Workgroup on Transportation Contract Approval Authority and serves as one of the three members of the Board of Public Works, whose oversight authority is the subject of the study.

The State Treasurer is a designated member of the Workgroup on Transportation Contract Approval Authority and serves as one of the three members of the Board of Public Works, whose oversight authority is the subject of the study.

The Governor is responsible for appointing several members of the workgroup, designating the chair, and receiving the final report and recommendations. Additionally, the Governor serves on the Board of Public Works, which is a primary focus of the study.

As the primary legal representative for state agencies, the OAG will likely provide legal counsel regarding the statutory changes to procurement authority and Board of Public Works jurisdiction being studied by the workgroup.

The Department of General Services is the state's central procurement authority and was consulted as an information source during the fiscal analysis. Changes to the Board of Public Works' procurement oversight structure may impact broader state procurement policy managed by DGS.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires a member of the workgroup to be a business owner certified as a Disadvantaged Business Enterprise (DBE) and a Minority Business Enterprise (MBE). This office oversees these specific socioeconomic procurement programs which are integral to the transportation contracts being studied.

bill_summary: This bill renames the Howard County Agricultural Land Preservation Fund to the Howard County Agricultural Preservation and Innovation Fund and expands the allowable use of its funds. In addition to agricultural land preservation, the proceeds may now be used for programs, services, or initiatives intended to enhance the commercial viability or environmental sustainability of agriculture in Howard County.
responsible_party: Howard County Director of Finance and the Howard County Council
stakeholders: Agricultural land owners, farmers, and the agricultural business community in Howard County
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no direct impact on State or local finances, as it does not change the local transfer tax rate or the percentage of revenue allocated to the fund. It only renames the fund and broadens the permitted uses of the existing revenue stream. According to the fiscal note, Howard County's fiscal 2026 budget allocates approximately $7,800,000 in transfer tax revenue to this fund.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill focuses on agricultural land preservation and enhancing the commercial viability and environmental sustainability of farming, which are core components of the Maryland Department of Agriculture's mission.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's expansion of the Howard County fund's scope to include 'innovation' and 'commercial viability' directly mirrors MARBIDCO's mission to support the profitability and sustainability of Maryland's agricultural industries through targeted financial services and partnerships.

The Department of Planning is responsible for land use planning and environmental preservation. Alterations to local agricultural land preservation funds are relevant to the state's broader strategies for sustainable growth and land resource management.
The bill aligns with this multi-agency initiative's goals of preserving farmland, protecting the environment, and promoting sustainable development through coordinated land-use planning.

The bill mentions using proceeds for the 'environmental sustainability' of agriculture, which intersects with the Department of the Environment's role in implementing state environmental laws and protecting natural resources.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives; the Governor signed this bill into law, making it relevant to the executive's legislative agenda for local and state-level agricultural support.

The Rural Maryland Council advocates for rural interests and agriculture. Since Howard County contains rural agricultural areas, the council has a general interest in policies affecting local agricultural funding and innovation.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits individuals in Wicomico County from standing in roadways, shoulders, median dividers, or intersections that the county or a municipality has determined to be 'inherently dangerous' in consultation with the Maryland State Highway Administration. It mandates the installation of appropriate warning signs before a police officer can issue a citation for a violation of the act.
responsible_party: Wicomico County, municipal corporations within Wicomico County, and the Maryland State Highway Administration
stakeholders: Pedestrians, motorists, and law enforcement officers in Wicomico County
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local operations or finances. The State Highway Administration can manage the bill's requirements using existing resources, and Wicomico County's finances are not expected to be significantly impacted.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires Wicomico County to consult with the State Highway Administration to determine if a State roadway is 'inherently dangerous' and mandates that any signs installed on State highways must have SHA's approval.

As the parent agency of the State Highway Administration (SHA), the Department of Transportation oversees the broader transportation policy and infrastructure standards impacted by this bill in Wicomico County.

As the primary law enforcement agency for state highways, the Maryland State Police will be responsible for enforcing the new standing prohibition and issuing citations in accordance with the bill's conditions.

The bill creates a new violation within the Transportation Article; the Administrative Office of the Courts will oversee the judicial processing and adjudication of any citations issued for these violations.
The bill addresses a specific public safety and community management issue in Wicomico County, which is one of the 18 rural counties supported and advocated for by the Rural Maryland Council.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the State Highway Administration and the Maryland State Police, and may be required to interpret the new statutory language or signage requirements.

As an agency within the Department of Transportation that manages driving records and traffic safety, the MVA may be minimally impacted by the creation of new roadway violations, even if primarily pedestrian-focused.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits unauthorized access to or interference with critical infrastructure and public safety answering points (PSAPs). It defines critical infrastructure as systems and assets vital to the State, such as those related to public security, health, and utilities, and establishes new felony offenses and penalties for actions intended to interrupt or impair these services.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Operators of critical infrastructure including public utilities, transportation, and health care facilities; public safety answering point (9-1-1 center) personnel; and law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The formal fiscal note indicates that the bill is not expected to materially affect State or local finances or operations. While the bill establishes new felony penalties and potential fines of up to $50,000, specific dollar estimates for total revenue or expenditure changes are unavailable as the overall fiscal impact is projected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department oversees the Maryland 9-1-1 Board and coordinates preparedness for emergencies. The bill specifically addresses interference with public safety answering points (PSAPs), which are central to the state's 9-1-1 system.

The department is responsible for the state's cybersecurity and IT infrastructure. The bill targets unauthorized access to computer networks and virtual assets, which falls directly under the agency's security and strategy mandate.
As the primary law enforcement agency for the state, the Maryland State Police are responsible for investigating criminal violations of the state's computer laws and ensuring public peace.

This office coordinates homeland security efforts and assesses readiness for emergencies. Protecting critical infrastructure from intentional interference is a core component of its disaster prevention strategy.
The bill's definition of 'critical infrastructure' explicitly includes public transportation systems. The department operates major transit networks that could be impacted by such interference.
The commission regulates public utilities such as electricity and natural gas. These services are specifically named in the bill as critical infrastructure components subject to protection.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency regulates the state's emergency medical services network and communications infrastructure, which relies on the functionality of public safety answering points.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department manages correctional facilities and public safety security. Additionally, the bill creates new felony penalties that directly affect the correctional population managed by the agency.
The agency provides operational and legal support to the judicial branch, which will process the criminal cases and felony prosecutions resulting from violations of this bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office provides legal representation to indigent defendants. The creation of new felony offenses for infrastructure interference will impact the agency's caseload.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies and manages public safety funds. The bill's focus on new criminal offenses for infrastructure interference aligns with its policy mandate.
The OAG is the chief legal representative for the state and provides counsel to agencies involved in infrastructure protection and law enforcement.
The department oversees public water and wastewater systems, which are included in the bill's definition of critical infrastructure related to public utilities.
The agency coordinates energy planning and policy. Electricity and natural gas services are specifically identified as critical infrastructure in the context of this legislation.
The bill defines critical infrastructure to include assets vital to public health and specifically mentions health care facilities, which are regulated by the department.
As the primary manager of state-owned facilities and physical infrastructure, the department is responsible for the security and maintenance of the types of assets the bill seeks to protect.
The office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. The Governor signed the bill and oversees the departments tasked with protecting critical infrastructure.
The bill's framework and the expanded infrastructure definitions include public schools. The agency provides coordination for school safety across the state.
The office advocates for utility consumers. Since the bill concerns the reliability and integrity of public utility infrastructure (electric/gas), it is relevant to consumer interests.

bill_summary: This bill updates the Maryland Uniform Simultaneous Death Act to align with the 1993 version of the uniform act. It establishes a requirement that an individual must be proven by clear and convincing evidence to have survived another person or a specific event by at least 120 hours to be legally recognized as a survivor for property inheritance and distribution. The bill also sets evidentiary standards for determining death, creates a presumption of death after a five-year absence, and provides liability protections for third-party payors who distribute assets in good faith reliance on governing instruments.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary (Administrative Office of the Courts), Orphans' Courts, and the Register of Wills
stakeholders: Heirs, beneficiaries of estates and insurance policies, co-owners of property with rights of survivorship (joint tenants), and third-party payors such as trustees and insurance companies.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill does not materially affect State or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Register of Wills is primarily responsible for the administrative probate of estates, including the timely administration of decedents' estates and the collection of inheritance taxes. This bill fundamentally changes the legal standard for determining survivorship (the 120-hour rule) for property distribution, which is a core function of the probate process managed by this agency.

The bill establishes evidentiary procedures for determining death or survival and deals with the distribution of disputed assets within the court system. The AOC provides operational and legal support to the Maryland Judicial Branch, which will adjudicate disputes arising from these new statutory requirements.

The bill explicitly includes insurers as 'payors' and identifies insurance policies as 'governing instruments.' It provides specific rules for how insurance proceeds should be distributed when survival cannot be established, which falls under the regulatory purview of the MIA.

The bill defines 'governing instruments' to include retirement or similar benefit plans and defines 'payors' to include government agencies. The SRA manages death benefits for state employees and teachers, and this bill's 120-hour survival requirement would govern the distribution of these benefits in simultaneous death scenarios.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly on the implementation and interpretation of new laws, including the Uniform Simultaneous Death Act.

The bill mentions escheatment to the State under certain conditions. The Comptroller's office manages unclaimed property and state revenues, which may be impacted if property lacks eligible heirs under the new 120-hour survival rule.

The bill defines 'payor' to include government agencies and 'governing instrument' to include retirement and benefit plans. As the central agency for state employee benefits, DBM has a secondary interest in how survival rules affect benefit payouts.

The bill references specific sections of the Health - General Article regarding the determination of death and the issuance of death certificates, which are managed by the Maryland Department of Health.
