bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) to expand its annual reporting on children in the state child welfare system to include college enrollment and six-year graduation rates for foster youth. It also mandates that MSDE, in cooperation with the Department of Human Services (DHS), submit a one-time report by December 1, 2026, that identifies service gaps and provides recommendations to improve educational outcomes and data collection for students in the foster care system, including comparison data for students not in the system.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education and the Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Children and foster youth in the Maryland child welfare system
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill has no state or local fiscal impact. Both the Maryland State Department of Education and the Department of Human Services are expected to meet the reporting requirements using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill primary tasks the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) with reporting annual data on foster youth outcomes and, in cooperation with the Department of Human Services, developing a comprehensive report on improving outcomes for students in the child welfare system.

As the primary agency for the State child welfare system, the Department of Human Services (DHS) is required to cooperate with MSDE in developing a report on improving educational outcomes for foster youth and will be a primary recipient of the data collected.

The Maryland Longitudinal Data System Center (MLDSC) is identified as a primary data source for the bill's requirements, specifically for linking foster care status with postsecondary enrollment and graduation data.

The Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC) is involved in tracking the college enrollment and graduation data required by the bill and is listed as a primary information source for the fiscal analysis.

The bill requires a report to identify all state agencies providing services for foster youth and to recommend improvements for their outcomes; the Governor's Office for Children is a central coordinating body for such policies.
As the state's public higher education system, USM is a stakeholder in the bill's requirements to track and improve the college enrollment and graduation rates of foster youth.
As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State University is a stakeholder in the tracking of foster youth postsecondary outcomes and educational readiness.
As a public institution of higher education, Saint Mary's College is a stakeholder in the tracking of foster youth postsecondary outcomes and educational readiness.

The population of youth in the juvenile justice system often overlaps with the child welfare system; DJS is likely one of the agencies providing services that must be identified in the required report.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates youth programs and public safety policies that intersect with the foster youth population, particularly regarding the reporting of school-based arrests.
The judiciary plays a critical role in the child welfare system (CINA cases), and judicial data or cooperation may be relevant to the comprehensive report on improving youth outcomes.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MSDE and DHS regarding the confidentiality of child welfare data and the legal requirements for reporting and information sharing established by the bill.
DBM oversees the resources for the implementing agencies; although the fiscal note indicates no new state effect, the agency maintains oversight of the fiscal health of the reporting departments.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the Maryland Child Care Scholarship (CCS) Program by altering eligibility, the application process, and copayment structures. It prohibits enrollment freezes for specific groups including homeless children and families receiving TANF or SSI, requires a waitlist with priority for children under age 3, and mandates that the State Department of Education assist applicants in accessing other programs like Head Start or publicly funded prekindergarten. Additionally, it repeals the process for presumptive eligibility and establishes a sliding copayment scale capped at 7% of household income, while exempting families at or below the federal poverty line from paying any copay.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE)
stakeholders: Low-income families, children under age 3, homeless children, child care providers, and recipients of government assistance programs such as TANF, TCA, and SSI.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures increase by $749,700 in FY 2027, which includes $650,000 for one-time contractual services for programming changes and costs for one new program manager. Ongoing administrative costs range from $118,200 in FY 2028 to $134,800 in FY 2031. The implementation of a sliding fee scale for copayments is expected to offset the cost of serving additional families, potentially allowing more than 1,000 additional children to receive scholarships annually without further increasing program expenditures. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is the primary agency responsible for administering the Child Care Scholarship Program. The bill mandates significant changes to MSDE's application processes, waitlist management, copayment structures, and requires them to provide assistance for Pre-K and Head Start enrollment. The fiscal note indicates MSDE will incur substantial costs for staffing and IT programming.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for state budget development and personnel. The bill mandates specific Governor-led appropriations for the scholarship program and requires MSDE to report on fiscal impacts, cost estimates, and reimbursement rates, which directly involves DBM's oversight of fiscal planning.

The Board of Public Works is explicitly mentioned in the bill as the authority required to approve budget reductions for the Program before the Department can implement certain emergency measures, such as reducing reimbursement rates or freezing enrollment.

The bill mandates that the Comptroller pay child care providers within five days of receiving notice from MSDE. As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller also oversees the fiscal integrity of the program and potential budget reductions mentioned in the bill.

The State Treasurer serves on the Board of Public Works, which must approve program budget reductions. Additionally, while certain sections are repealed, the Treasurer generally manages the state funds from which these scholarships and related administrative costs are paid.

The bill defines eligibility exemptions for enrollment freezes based on participation in programs administered by the Department of Human Services, specifically Temporary Cash Assistance (TCA) and TANF. MSDE is also required to provide information on government assistance programs, necessitating coordination with DHS.

The bill requires the Governor to include specific minimum appropriations in the annual State budget for the Child Care Scholarship Program and involves executive branch policy coordination regarding child care and poverty.

The Governor's Office for Children is focused on reducing child poverty and improving access to health and education services. This bill directly impacts child care access and economic mobility for low-income families, which are core priorities of the office and its ENOUGH Initiative.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires MSDE to consult with the Office of Child Care Advisory Council when conducting market rate analyses for reimbursement rates. This Council is an advisory body within the executive branch tasked with providing expertise on child care issues.

The Innovation Team is charged with piloting novel initiatives to address the Governor's priorities of reducing child poverty and enhancing economic mobility. The major changes to the Child Care Scholarship Program in this bill align directly with these objectives.

responsible_party: Maryland Department of Natural Resources
stakeholders: Archery hunters and property owners in Baltimore City
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local government finances are not expected to be materially affected by the bill's changes to archery safety zones. The impact on small businesses is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Natural Resources Article regarding hunting safety zones. The Department of Natural Resources is the primary agency responsible for managing wildlife and enforcing conservation and hunting laws through the Natural Resources Police.
As the head of the executive branch, the Governor oversees the Department of Natural Resources and is responsible for signing the bill into law or vetoing it.
The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Natural Resources and the State regarding the enforcement and interpretation of natural resources laws and regulations.

bill_summary: This bill expands the authority of the Maryland Department of Human Services to disclose reports or records of child abuse or neglect to certain entities for the purpose of background checks. Specifically, it allows disclosure to administrators of government-run child care centers, youth sports program managers, and organizations supervising children to determine an individual's suitability for employment or volunteer service, provided there is a finalized finding of indicated abuse or neglect.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Applicants for employment or volunteer positions in child care and youth sports, administrators and coaches of youth sports programs, child care center operators, and the Department of Human Services.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures could increase by an estimated $567,000 annually if the Department of Human Services (DHS) requires additional staff to process disclosure requests, as estimated by DHS. However, the Department of Legislative Services suggests the bill can likely be implemented using existing resources. There is no expected impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DHS is the primary agency responsible for managing the centralized confidential database of child abuse and neglect records and is explicitly authorized by the bill to disclose these reports and records to newly specified individuals and organizations.

The bill expands the disclosure of child abuse records to school superintendents and principals for personnel actions and references the licensing of child care centers and family child care providers, which falls under MSDE's oversight.

The bill explicitly names the Chancellor of the University System of Maryland as an individual authorized to receive reports and records of child abuse to carry out personnel or administrative actions following reports involving employees or contractors.

The bill identifies state officials responsible for juvenile services as authorized recipients of child abuse records and addresses the Juvenile Justice Monitoring Unit, which oversees DJS facilities.

The bill transfers the Juvenile Justice Monitoring Unit from the Office of the Attorney General to the Office of the Correctional Ombudsman. Additionally, the OAG provides legal counsel to many of the agencies involved in implementing these disclosure changes.

The bill addresses the disclosure of records to licensed practitioners at hospitals and birthing centers (which are regulated by MDH) to assist in making discharge decisions when child safety is a concern.
The bill expands disclosure permissions to administrators of child care centers located in State-occupied buildings, which are managed and maintained by DGS.

As the coordinating board for postsecondary education, this agency is relevant to the bill's provisions regarding personnel and administrative actions at Maryland public institutions of higher education following child abuse reports.

As a public institution of higher education, its president is authorized under the bill to receive child abuse reports for personnel or administrative actions concerning employees or volunteers with on-campus contact with children.

As a public institution of higher education, its leadership is authorized to receive child abuse reports to manage personnel and administrative actions involving staff or contractors with access to children.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mentions the State Council on Child Abuse and Neglect and the State Citizens Review Board for Children as entities authorized to receive child abuse reports to carry out their official functions.
DBM is relevant due to the fiscal and personnel implications for the Department of Human Services, which requested additional staff to manage the increased volume of disclosure requests.

The agency's role in coordinating school safety is relevant to the bill's provisions regarding the disclosure of abuse records to school leadership for administrative and personnel actions to protect students.
The bill's focus on child welfare and the protection of children from abuse and neglect aligns with the mission of this office to promote the well-being of Maryland's children.

Synopsis: Altering, beginning in taxable year 2027, the homeowners' property tax credit application cycle to be year-round for each taxable year; and applying the Act to all taxable years beginning after June 30, 2027.
Title: Homeowners’ Property Tax Credit – Year–Round Application
bill_summary: This bill alters the application process for the Maryland Homeowners' Property Tax Credit to a year-round cycle, allowing homeowners to apply for the credit through February 14 of the taxable year for which the credit is sought.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Maryland homeowners meeting specific income and net worth requirements who are eligible for the property tax credit.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note estimates that State general fund expenditures will increase by approximately 168200 annually beginning in fiscal 2028. Local government revenues may decrease in jurisdictions that provide supplemental homeowners' property tax credits, including Baltimore City and 13 counties, to the extent that more homeowners qualify for the credit due to the extended application timeline.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This board is explicitly tasked with hearing appeals regarding property tax assessments and various property tax credits; the alteration of the application cycle for the homeowners' property tax credit is directly within its area of administrative review for contested cases.

The bill is projected to increase state general fund expenditures by approximately $168,200 annually starting in fiscal 2028, requiring DBM to manage the fiscal impact and budget execution for the program.

As an independent agency performing quasi-judicial functions for tax disputes, including real property assessments and final decisions of taxing authorities, it would adjudicate escalated appeals related to eligibility or denials under the new year-round application process.

The homeowners' property tax credit is a significant financial benefit for older adults, and the bill contains specific provisions relating to applicants over 70 years of age and those with pension or social security income.

The Governor's Office is responsible for proposing the annual state budget, which must accommodate the increased general fund expenditures resulting from the expanded application window for the tax credit.

As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller oversees the fiscal health and revenue management of the state, which is impacted by the increased expenditures on the homeowners' property tax credit.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the state agencies responsible for administering tax laws and would offer guidance on the implementation and regulatory enforcement of the new year-round application cycle.

As the state's central personnel agency, DBM is directly impacted by the bill's requirement for recommendations on updated IT classifications and pay scales, and will likely be involved in the implementation of the study's personnel-related findings.
The Governor's Office is a recipient of the final study and, as a principal department (the Executive Department), its own IT staffing and environment will be subject to assessment under the bill.
The OAG will likely provide legal counsel regarding the procurement of the third-party entity to ensure the contract complies with state law.

bill_summary: This bill establishes that any provision in a trust (an in terrorem clause) that attempts to penalize an interested person for contesting the trust or starting legal proceedings related to the estate is void if probable cause exists for taking such action.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and the Register of Wills
stakeholders: Trust beneficiaries, trustees, and individuals involved in trust-related legal proceedings
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government finances. No specific revenue changes or expenditure mandates are identified.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes legal standards for trust provisions that are void under certain circumstances, which directly impacts judicial proceedings and the administration of justice within the state court system.

The Register of Wills is responsible for administrative probate and serves as Clerk to the Orphans' Court. Because the bill affects proceedings relating to trusts and estates, it is relevant to their administrative and record-keeping duties.
As the state's chief legal officer, the OAG provides counsel to the Judiciary and the General Assembly on the interpretation of state laws, including amendments to the Estates and Trusts Article.
The Governor's Office is responsible for overseeing the executive branch and signing legislation into law. This bill requires the Governor's approval to amend the Maryland Trust Act.

Synopsis: Establishing an expedited processing fee for certain documents filed with the State Department of Assessments and Taxation; and requiring the Department to process documents filed at least 1 hour before the Department's close of business within 1 hour after the documents are received.
Title: State Department of Assessments and Taxation - Expedited Document Processing and Fees

bill_summary: This bill establishes new expedited processing tiers and associated fees for documents filed with the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT). It specifically creates a 1-hour processing window for a $1,000 fee and a 30-minute processing window for a $1,500 fee, provided the documents have first been accepted for preclearance. It also updates the existing 2-hour expedited processing fee to $425.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Business entities, large law firms, and other parties filing corporate documents that require time-sensitive processing.
fiscal_impact_summary: The State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) can implement the bill with existing resources. State special fund revenues are expected to increase starting in fiscal 2028 from the new expedited filing fees ($1,000 for 1-hour and $1,500 for 30-minute processing). While the total revenue increase is indeterminate and depends on the volume of filings, the Fiscal Note provides an illustrative estimate that every 100 filings at the 1-hour tier would generate approximately 85000 in additional revenue. Local government finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that $50 of the $150 processing fee collected for certain nonstock corporations be credited to the Maryland Nonprofit Development Center Program Fund. This fund is established under the Economic Development Article and supports programs typically overseen by the Department of Commerce.

The bill explicitly references the employer-offered savings arrangement definition in the Labor and Employment Article to maintain a filing fee waiver for entities that participate in the MarylandSaves program or provide equivalent retirement savings options.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and fiscal planning. The bill establishes new tiered expedited processing fees that the fiscal note projects will increase special fund revenues.

The Treasurer's Office is the chief financial agency responsible for the management and protection of state funds. It will be responsible for receiving and depositing the increased special fund revenues generated by the new fee tiers.

The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for all state agencies. It would be responsible for providing legal counsel to the State Department of Assessments and Taxation regarding the implementation of the new fee structure and the adoption of required regulations.

bill_summary: The Maryland Stablecoin Act establishes a regulatory and legal framework for businesses providing payment stablecoin services in Maryland. It requires nondepository trust companies and credit union service organizations to obtain a certificate from the Office of Financial Regulation to operate as payment stablecoin service institutions or state issuers. The bill also aligns Maryland law with the federal GENIUS Act of 2025 and reduces the examination fee for new commercial bank charters from $15,000 to $7,000.
responsible_party: Office of Financial Regulation (OFR) within the Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Financial institutions including nondepository trust companies, credit union service organizations, commercial banks, and credit unions, as well as consumers using digital payment stablecoin services.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Office of Financial Regulation can implement the bill's provisions using existing budgeted resources. State special fund revenues are not expected to be materially affected; while the examination fee for new commercial bank charters is reduced by $8,000 per instance, these applications are infrequent and any lost revenue is expected to be recovered through annual assessments on the regulated institutions. There is no significant impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor's Office of Financial Regulation (OFR) is the primary implementing agency for the Maryland Stablecoin Act. The Commissioner of Financial Regulation is designated as the State Payment Stablecoin Regulator, responsible for certifying issuers, conducting examinations, and enforcing the regulatory framework established under the new Title 14.

The Office of the Attorney General provides primary legal counsel to the Commissioner of Financial Regulation and would represent the state in enforcement actions or legal challenges related to the oversight of stablecoin institutions.

The bill explicitly references the right to a hearing under the Administrative Procedure Act for entities contesting the denial or revocation of a certificate, a function performed by Administrative Law Judges at the OAH.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments involved in this new regulatory framework and is responsible for the overall coordination of financial and economic policy initiatives within the state.
The establishment of a regulatory framework for digital assets like stablecoins directly impacts Maryland's economic competitiveness and attractiveness to financial technology (fintech) businesses.

As the state's chief financial agency, the Treasurer's Office has a significant interest in the management and protection of financial assets and the regulatory environment governing financial institutions and digital payment systems.

Stablecoins are digital assets reliant on blockchain technology and complex IT infrastructure; DoIT oversees the state's overarching information technology and cybersecurity strategy which intersects with the regulation of digital assets.

TEDCO supports early-stage technology-based businesses; the regulation of payment stablecoins directly affects the regulatory environment for Maryland fintech startups that TEDCO may support or invest in.

The Comptroller, as the state's chief financial officer, maintains a general interest in laws affecting financial institutions and the potential tax and revenue implications of newly regulated asset classes.

bill_summary: Requires manufacturers of menstrual hygiene products to list all ingredients on the packaging of products sold in Maryland beginning April 1, 2028. The ingredient list must be displayed prominently in order of predominance. Violations are considered unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices and are subject to civil penalties of up to $1,000.
responsible_party: Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
stakeholders: Manufacturers of menstrual hygiene products and consumers in Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues may increase minimally from civil penalties of up to $1,000 established for violations of the labeling requirements. The Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division can implement the bill with existing resources, and collected penalties are intended to offset enforcement costs. There is no material impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General as the primary enforcement body. It classifies violations as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices and empowers the Division to collect and process civil penalties.

As the agency responsible for public health and safety, the Department of Health is relevant to policies governing health-related products like menstrual hygiene items, and the bill was considered by health-focused committees in the General Assembly.

The Office of Administrative Hearings provides an impartial hearing process for contested cases involving state agencies; it would likely adjudicate disputes arising from enforcement actions or penalties imposed by the OAG under this legislation.
Violations of the Maryland Consumer Protection Act can lead to civil actions in state courts, and the bill establishes a civil penalty that may be subject to judicial adjudication.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments involved in enforcement and is responsible for final approval of the legislation.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees state revenues and agency resources; the fiscal note indicates that penalties will be paid into the general fund and that OAG will manage enforcement within its existing budget.

Synopsis: Requiring certain centers where mammography testing is performed to include in the screening results letter that is sent to a patient, as required by federal law, a notice of the presence of arterial calcification as observed during the patient's mammogram.

bill_summary: This bill requires mammography centers to include a specific notice in a patient's screening results letter if breast arterial calcification is observed. The notice informs patients that while breast arterial calcification is a common finding, it may be an indicator of an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and advises them to discuss the results with their physician to assess cardiovascular risks.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Patients receiving mammograms, healthcare providers, and mammography centers including hospitals and clinics
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local finances or operations. Small business impact is estimated to be minimal. The Maryland Department of Health may adopt regulations to update the notice content if medical evidence changes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary agency responsible for overseeing the bill's implementation. Under the bill, 'The Department' is specifically authorized to adopt regulations to change the content of the arterial calcification notice if current medical evidence changes.

As an independent regulatory agency within MDH, the MHCC is responsible for health system planning and promoting informed decision-making for patients. The bill's requirement for mammography centers to provide specific diagnostic information directly impacts the commission's mission regarding health quality and patient access to information.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the State of Maryland and provides legal counsel to MDH. It would be involved in reviewing and drafting any regulations the Department adopts to modify the mandatory patient notices.

The University System of Maryland operates extensive clinical facilities and academic medical centers. These centers perform mammography testing and would be required to update their administrative procedures and screening results letters to include the mandated notice.

bill_summary: This bill requires health insurance carriers to provide coverage for the evaluation and management of menopause and associated symptoms. It mandates that health occupations boards grant double continuing education credits (two hours for every one hour of training) for menopause-related education. Additionally, the bill requires the Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland Commission for Women to evaluate and report on state policy initiatives, clinical education opportunities, and methods to increase access to menopause-related healthcare services.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland Commission for Women
stakeholders: Individuals experiencing perimenopause, menopause, and postmenopause; healthcare providers; and health insurance carriers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $100,300 in FY 2027 and $30,200 in FY 2028 for the Maryland Department of Health to hire a part-time contractual health policy analyst and a vendor to complete required evaluations and reports. Special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration increase minimally in FY 2027 due to $125 rate and form filing fees. Local governments may experience increased health care expenditures if they purchase fully insured health plans. The State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program is expected to see no material impact as it already covers these services.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDH is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation. It must identify training programs, consult with health occupations boards on continuing education, evaluate access to menopause health care with community health workers, and evaluate methods for clinical education in higher education institutions.

MIA is responsible for regulating the insurance market and ensuring that insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and HMOs comply with the new mandate to provide coverage for the evaluation and management of menopause.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly alters the membership and statutory duties of the State Advisory Council on Health and Wellness. It also tasks the Maryland Commission for Women with conducting a major study on policy initiatives to improve health and economic security.
The Maryland Commission for Women is administratively housed within DHS. The bill tasks the Commission with evaluating state policy initiatives and reporting findings to the General Assembly.
DBM oversees the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program. The fiscal note indicates the department evaluated the impact of the new insurance mandate on the state plan.
The Secretary of Aging is a permanent member of the State Advisory Council on Health and Wellness, whose membership and structure are modified by this bill.
The Secretary of Disabilities is a permanent member of the State Advisory Council on Health and Wellness, which is being reorganized under the bill.
The State Superintendent of Schools is a permanent member of the State Advisory Council on Health and Wellness, which is being reorganized under the bill.
The bill requires MDH to consult with institutions of higher education to evaluate methods for increasing clinical education on menopause; the Commission coordinates these institutions.
The USM and its member institutions are potential entities for consultation by MDH regarding clinical and postgraduate education methods for menopause treatment.
As a public research university, Morgan State may be consulted by MDH regarding clinical education and treatment methods for menopause as required by Section 5 of the bill.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments (MDH, DHS) and coordinates the policy initiatives related to public health and women's health addressed in the bill.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MDH and the health occupations boards as they develop new regulations for continuing education and implement new statutory requirements.

Synopsis: Establishing a Commission on Re-Imagining Health Care to envision and make recommendations regarding establishing a comprehensive, patient-centered  health care system in the State; and requiring the Commission to submit a preliminary report by December 1, 2027, and a final report of the Commission's findings and recommendations to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2029.
Title: Commission on Re-Imagining Health Care in Maryland

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Commission on Re-Imagining Health Care in Maryland to envision and make recommendations for a comprehensive, patient-centered health care system that integrates somatic, behavioral, dental, vision, and hearing services. The commission is tasked with studying global delivery models, reimbursement rates, and insurance barriers to suggest improvements to the State's health care infrastructure.
responsible_party: Maryland Health Care Commission
stakeholders: Maryland residents, health care practitioners, health insurance carriers, hospitals, managed care organizations, and state and local health agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's implementation is contingent upon the Maryland Health Care Commission securing private funding. If sufficient private funding is secured and notice is provided to the Department of Legislative Services by June 1, 2027, special fund revenues and expenditures will increase by an indeterminate amount between fiscal 2027 and 2030. These funds would support commission operations, including potential contractual staff and reporting requirements. No local fiscal impact is anticipated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Health Care Commission (MHCC) is the primary implementing agency. The bill mandates that MHCC provide staff for the Commission, determine the required funding levels, and secure private funding to enable the Commission to function. The Executive Director of MHCC is also a named member.

The Secretary of Health and the Deputy Secretary of Health Care Financing (Medicaid) are named members of the Commission. The Commission's goal to re-imagine the entire state health care system, including somatic and behavioral health, directly aligns with the Department's core mission and regulatory scope.

The Governor's Office is responsible for appointing 11 members of the Commission, jointly designating the chair, and receiving the Commission's preliminary and final reports. The Commission's findings will likely shape future health policy initiatives proposed by the Executive Department.

The Secretary of Budget and Management is a named member of the Commission. The agency's involvement is critical because the Commission is tasked with envisioning a system that is 'financially sustainable.'

The Maryland Insurance Commissioner is a named member of the Commission. The Commission's study includes analyzing how health insurance deductibles and networks affect care, which falls under the MIA's regulatory oversight.

The Executive Director of the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange is a named member of the Commission. The Commission's focus on universal access and eliminating barriers to care is central to the Exchange's mission of providing accessible and affordable health coverage.

The Executive Director of the HSCRC is a named member of the Commission. The Commission's study of hospital roles and the cost-balance of the health care system is directly relevant to the HSCRC's authority over hospital rate-setting and hospital-payer systems.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill establishes a new Commission on Re-Imagining Health Care in Maryland, which fits the definition of this collective entity as a temporary body created by the General Assembly to address specific government policy issues.
The bill specifically requires the Commission to study 'the role of the worker's compensation program in an integrated system,' making it directly relevant to this agency's mandate.
The Office of Appointments will assist the Governor in recruiting and vetting the 11 specific representatives and public members appointed to the Commission.

The Commission is tasked with studying 'new models of health care practitioner education and development,' which falls under the regulatory and policy-making purview of the Maryland Higher Education Commission regarding academic programs and financial aid for students in these fields.

As the provider of much of the state's medical and health practitioner education, USM is directly impacted by the Commission's mandate to study new models of education and development for health care practitioners.

The OAG will likely provide legal counsel to the Commission and the various state agencies (MDH, MHCC, MIA, etc.) involved in drafting the recommendations and interpreting the requirements of the bill.

Synopsis: Establishing the Audit and Finance Compliance Unit in the Department of Budget and Management; requiring the Governor to implement systems and processes to monitor certain efforts; requiring the Unit to monitor efforts of Departmental Units to correct certain audit findings and provide guidance, coordination, and technical assistance; authorizing the Unit to implement steps to address and prevent audit findings; requiring the Unit to provide direct assistance to Departmental Units with four or more repeat audit findings; etc.
Title: Department of Budget and Management - Audit and Finance Compliance Unit - Establishment

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Audit and Finance Compliance Unit (AFCU) within the Department of Budget and Management to monitor and assist Executive Branch agencies in correcting audit findings reported by the Office of Legislative Audits. The unit provides technical assistance, guidance, and coordination to strengthen internal controls and requires an annual report on the progress of corrective actions to the Joint Audit and Evaluation Committee.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Budget and Management
stakeholders: Executive Branch departmental units, State employees, and the Joint Audit and Evaluation Committee
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures increase by $216,971 in FY 2026 and by $2,288,120 in FY 2027 to establish and staff the Audit and Finance Compliance Unit. These costs include nine additional regular positions and $650,000 in annual contractor costs. Future years reflect ongoing personnel and operating costs, estimated between $2,140,000 and $2,350,000 through FY 2031. There is no impact on local government finances or state revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Audit and Finance Compliance Unit (AFCU) within the Department of Budget and Management (DBM). DBM is the primary agency responsible for monitoring audit findings across the executive branch and has received significant contingent appropriations to staff the new unit.

The bill requires the Governor to implement systems and processes to monitor audit corrective actions. Furthermore, the Governor, Chief of Staff, and Deputy Chiefs of Staff are granted access to view unredacted cybersecurity findings.

The bill deals specifically with unredacted cybersecurity findings, and the fiscal note indicates DoIT is piloting a management tool to track audit findings. DoIT is also specifically identified as an agency with repeat audit findings requiring monitoring.

The bill re-enacts and modifies statutory language requiring the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Maryland to implement monitoring systems for the Judiciary's audit findings, which is supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The Comptroller's office is specifically identified in the fiscal note as an executive unit with repeat audit findings in 2024, making it a primary subject of the new monitoring and technical assistance unit.

The Department of General Services is explicitly mentioned in the fiscal note as having repeat audit findings in 2025, which subjects it to oversight and direct assistance from the newly created AFCU.
The Maryland Department of Health is explicitly named as having repeat audit findings in both 2024 and 2025 reports, making it a key focus for the AFCU's direct assistance and monitoring efforts.
This agency was specifically identified in the fiscal note as having repeat audit findings in 2024, requiring monitoring and corrective action under the new AFCU framework.
The Department of Human Services is explicitly mentioned in the fiscal note as an agency with repeat audit findings in 2025, subjecting it to the bill's monitoring and assistance provisions.
The Department of Transportation is identified as an agency with repeat audit findings in 2024, making it a target for the AFCU's monitoring and technical assistance.
The college is specifically named in the fiscal note as an entity with repeat audit findings in 2024, placing it under the purview of the newly created monitoring systems within DBM.
As an executive departmental unit, the agency is subject to the Governor's new monitoring systems and potential oversight or assistance from the DBM Audit and Finance Compliance Unit.

Title: Public Health - Office of Health Care Quality Information and Maryland Health Centralization Commission

bill_summary: This emergency bill establishes the Maryland Health Centralization Commission to provide ongoing advice and recommendations on improving collaboration between the Maryland Department of Health and various health occupations boards to enhance efficiency, transparency, and accountability. It also requires the Maryland Health Care Commission, in collaboration with the Office of Health Care Quality, to publish facility inspection dates and quality metrics on the Maryland Quality Reporting website. Furthermore, it mandates that health occupations boards certify annually that their information technology systems meet state cybersecurity standards.
responsible_party: Maryland Health Centralization Commission, Maryland Health Care Commission, and the Department of Information Technology
stakeholders: Maryland Department of Health, health occupations boards, health care professionals, health care facilities, and the general public
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill's requirements can be handled with existing budgeted resources, and revenues are not affected. Commission members are entitled to reimbursement for travel expenses under standard regulations, but these costs are expected to be absorbed. The analysis does not account for potential future costs associated with implementing the commission's eventual recommendations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDH is the primary agency affected by the bill. Its Office of Health Care Quality must collaborate on publishing inspection data, the Secretary and Deputy Secretary serve on the newly created commission, and the bill focuses on the relationship between MDH and its health occupations boards.

MHCC is a primary implementing agency, required to collaborate with MDH to publish health facility inspection information and quality metrics on its public reporting website, and its future usage is a topic for the commission's recommendations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly establishes the Maryland Health Centralization Commission as a new body to study health board oversight and provide recommendations to the General Assembly.

The Secretary of Information Technology is given a new statutory oversight role to ensure health occupations boards comply with minimum cybersecurity standards and must receive annual certifications from those boards.
The bill was introduced based on OLA's fiscal compliance audit findings, and the new commission is specifically mandated to recommend how health boards can remedy OLA audit findings and violations.
The Governor receives annual reports from the new commission and oversees the executive branch departments (MDH, DoIT) tasked with implementing the bill's requirements.
The bill specifies that commission members are reimbursed via standard state travel regulations provided in the state budget, which DBM manages as the state's principal fiscal and personnel agency.

The commission's scope includes recommending policies for criminal history records checks and the receipt of information from the Central Repository, which involves records managed by the state's primary law enforcement and identification systems.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Medical Assistance Program and the Maryland Children's Health Program to provide a prior authorization determination regarding a transfer on request of a special pediatric hospital within 3 business days after the request is received; and requiring the Maryland Department of Health to adopt regulations on or before December 31, 2026, establishing a retrospective review process for special pediatric hospitals.
Title: Maryland Medical Assistance Program, Maryland Children's Health Program, and Health Insurance - Transfers to Special Pediatric Hospitals - Requirements

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) and the Maryland Children’s Health Program (MCHP) to provide a prior authorization determination within three business days for requested transfers to special pediatric hospitals. Additionally, it mandates that the Maryland Department of Health establish a retrospective review process by December 31, 2026, to allow special pediatric hospitals to appeal denied medical necessity determinations through peer-to-peer reconsideration and physician-led reviews.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Special pediatric hospitals, pediatric patients under age 22 (or up to age 23 with co-occurring physical and behavioral health conditions), referring health care providers, and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State Medicaid expenditures will increase by an indeterminate amount beginning in fiscal 2027, with costs split 50% from general funds and 50% from federal funds. This increase is attributed to necessary contract modifications for the Department's utilization control agent and the administrative and reimbursement costs associated with establishing a new retrospective review process. Federal fund revenues are expected to increase accordingly to cover the federal share of these expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) as it administers the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) and the Maryland Children’s Health Program (MCHP). The department is specifically required to provide prior authorization determinations and adopt regulations establishing a retrospective review process for special pediatric hospitals.

The bill has an indeterminate fiscal impact on Medicaid expenditures, which the Department of Budget and Management oversees as the state's principal fiscal agency. DBM is also listed as an information source in the fiscal note.

The Office of the Attorney General will be required to provide legal counsel to the Maryland Department of Health during the drafting of new regulations and represent the state in any administrative appeals resulting from the new retrospective review process.

The bill requires the retrospective review process to comply with the Administrative Procedure Act (Title 10, Subtitle 2 of the State Government Article). Contested medical necessity determinations would likely be adjudicated by Administrative Law Judges at this agency.

The bill involves prior authorization and medical necessity determinations for healthcare services. While focused on Medicaid/MCHP, the agency is listed as an information source and regulates the managed care organizations (MCOs) that implement these programs.

The bill affects special pediatric hospitals that provide services to individuals with physical and behavioral health conditions. This patient population aligns with the department's mission to coordinate services and improve delivery for Marylanders with disabilities.

As the chief executive's office, it oversees the Department of Health and is responsible for the final approval of the bill and the coordination of the policy initiative to improve pediatric healthcare access.

The agency is dedicated to the well-being of Maryland's children and families. This bill directly impacts health service delivery and administrative protections for vulnerable children requiring specialized hospital care.

Synopsis: Establishing the Redirecting Safe Prescription Drugs Pilot Program; requiring the Secretary of Health to collaborate with the federal Drug Enforcement Agency and certain drop-off sites in the State to separate and redirect certain prescription medications to a State repository program; and requiring each drop-off site participating in the Pilot Program to ensure that any prescription medications collected are packaged in a certain manner and transferred to a repository.
Title: Prescription Drug Repository Program - Redirecting Safe Prescription Drugs Pilot Program

NarrowSubjects.Name: Drugs -see also- Cannabis; ControlDangSubst; Pharm; etc.
Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Redirecting Safe Prescription Drugs Pilot Program to expand medication access for underserved populations and reduce pharmaceutical waste. The program requires the Secretary of Health to collaborate with the federal Drug Enforcement Agency and four drop-off sites to separate and redirect eligible, noncontrolled, unopened prescription medications collected during National Prescription Drug Take Back Day to the State's Prescription Drug Repository Program.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the State Board of Pharmacy
stakeholders: Underserved populations, participating pharmacies, health care facilities, and the federal Drug Enforcement Agency.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the Maryland Department of Health and the State Board of Pharmacy can handle any oversight or reporting responsibilities with existing budgeted resources. Revenues are not affected, and there is no fiscal impact on local governments. The impact on small businesses is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of Health is tasked with administering the Redirecting Safe Prescription Drugs Pilot Program, collaborating with federal authorities and drop-off sites, and reporting on the program's outcomes. The State Board of Pharmacy, which regulates the Prescription Drug Repository Program, is a unit within this department.

As a division of the Maryland Department of Health responsible for enforcing the state's Controlled Dangerous Substance Act and protecting residents from drug diversion, this office is highly relevant to a pilot program focused on separating controlled and non-controlled substances during collection.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the Board of Pharmacy. They would likely be involved in reviewing the legal framework for the collaboration between state drop-off sites and the federal Drug Enforcement Agency.

Maryland State Police frequently host and secure drop-off locations for National Prescription Drug Take Back Days. Since the pilot program specifically targets medications collected during these events, the agency is an operational stakeholder in the collection process.
One of the explicit purposes of the pilot program is to reduce pharmaceutical waste, which aligns with MDE's mission to implement environmental laws and protect land and water quality from pollution.

The Secretary of Health, who administers the program, serves at the pleasure of the Governor. The office oversees the executive branch's policy initiatives, and this pilot program represents a targeted health policy effort.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM monitors the implementation of programs by state agencies and ensures that MDH handles the pilot program within existing budgeted resources as noted in the fiscal note.

Synopsis: Altering the minimum commission rate from 10% to 5% of the total premium that the Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund is required to pay to a fund producer of a policyholder to whom a policy is issued for private passenger auto insurance; and prohibiting the Fund from paying a commission to a fund producer for a policy written directly by the Fund without the involvement of a fund producer.
Title: Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund - Fund Producer Commission Rate

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Health Insurance -see also- ACA; HMOs; MCOs

bill_summary: This bill reduces the minimum commission rate that the Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund (MAIF) must pay to insurance producers for private passenger auto insurance from 10% to 5% of the total premium. It also prohibits the Fund from paying commissions on insurance policies that are written directly by the Fund without the involvement of a producer.
responsible_party: Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund
stakeholders: Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund, insurance producers, and private passenger automobile insurance policyholders.
fiscal_impact_summary: MAIF nonbudgeted expenditures are estimated to decrease beginning in fiscal 2027, potentially by $250,000 or more annually, to the extent that the Fund utilizes its new authority to reduce producer commission rates. There is no material impact on State general fund operations or finances, and no local fiscal impact. Small businesses serving as insurance producers for MAIF may experience a meaningful decrease in revenue.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's insurer of last resort, MAIF is the primary entity affected by this bill. The legislation directly alters MAIF's statutory requirements regarding the commission rates it pays to insurance producers and prohibits it from paying commissions on policies written directly without producer involvement, which will lead to a decrease in its nonbudgeted expenditures.

The bill amends the Insurance Article of the Annotated Code of Maryland, which is the primary regulatory domain of the MIA. Furthermore, the bill affects the compensation of insurance producers, whom the MIA is responsible for licensing and regulating. The MIA also provided information for the bill's fiscal analysis.

The OAG serves as the primary legal counsel for state agencies, including MAIF. It would be responsible for providing legal guidance on the interpretation of the amended Insurance Article and representing MAIF in any potential litigation arising from changes to producer commission structures.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "abuse" to include female genital mutilation for the purposes of a provision of law requiring certain persons to provide notice of suspected abuse or neglect of a child or make a written report of suspected abuse or neglect of a child; altering the actions regarding female genital mutilation in which a person is prohibited from engaging; increasing the penalties for a violation of certain provisions related to female genital mutilation; etc.
Title: Public Health - Female Genital Mutilation

bill_summary: This bill updates the definition of child abuse to include female genital mutilation (FGM) and increases criminal penalties for performing or facilitating the procedure on a minor to a felony with up to 10 years imprisonment and a $10,000 fine. It mandates the revocation of professional licenses for healthcare providers convicted of FGM, permits victims to pursue civil damages, and tasks the Maryland Department of Health with creating educational materials and reporting annual statistics to the General Assembly.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Children under age 18, victims of female genital mutilation, licensed healthcare practitioners, parents or guardians, and law enforcement.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures are estimated to increase by $39,500 in FY 2027, $40,900 in FY 2028, and $17,900 in FY 2029 to fund a part-time contractual health policy analyst at the Maryland Department of Health. These costs cover the development of educational materials and the establishment of data collection procedures, with the position terminating in December 2028. No significant impact on local finances or small businesses is expected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new civil cause of action in circuit courts for victims of female genital mutilation and sets a statute of limitations for such actions, impacting court operations and the Judicial Branch's data tracking for required reports.

The fiscal note identifies a need for general fund expenditures and a new part-time contractual position to implement the bill's reporting and educational requirements, which falls under DBM's oversight of state budget and personnel.

Educators are mandatory reporters of child abuse, and this bill expands that definition to include female genital mutilation. MSDE is responsible for schools, which are designated recipients of the new educational materials developed by MDH.

MDH is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation, including collaborating with organizations to develop and distribute educational materials, collecting data, and submitting an annual report to the General Assembly.

DHS oversees the Social Services Administration, which must be consulted for the annual report. Local departments of human services are also responsible for investigating child abuse and neglect reports, the definition of which is expanded by this bill.

Staff members at juvenile detention centers are mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse; the bill's expansion of the definition of abuse to include female genital mutilation directly impacts their reporting protocols.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill increases criminal penalties to 10 years for a felony, which impacts state correctional facilities. Additionally, parole and probation officers (human service workers) are mandatory reporters under the Family Law Article.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive agencies (MDH, DHS, DPSCS) tasked with implementing and enforcing the new legal standards and reporting requirements regarding female genital mutilation.

The GOC coordinates policies dedicated to child well-being; the bill's focus on child abuse prevention and mandatory reporting for minors aligns with the office's mission to improve support networks for vulnerable youth.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates public safety strategies and advises on criminal justice policy. The bill's creation of new criminal penalties and interagency reporting requirements for a specific form of abuse is relevant to their policy coordination role.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note identifies HCADRO as an agency that provided information during the fiscal analysis of the bill, as it relates to health-related legal claims and alternative dispute processes.
State and local law enforcement agencies are mandatory reporters of child abuse and are involved in the investigation of suspected violations and the subsequent criminal prosecutions.

The bill requires health occupations licensing boards to revoke licenses for convictions related to female genital mutilation. Such disciplinary actions may be appealed to the OAH for an impartial hearing.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the health occupations boards and the Department of Health regarding the implementation of license revocation mandates and new reporting requirements.

Synopsis: Requiring, to make a claim under a warranty for certain agricultural equipment, a consumer to provide written notice to certain parties to report a nonconformity, defect, or condition occurring in certain agricultural equipment; requiring certain parties to correct the nonconformity, defect, or condition in a certain manner; and requiring certain parties to provide a consumer with the opportunity to replace agricultural equipment or receive a refund under certain circumstances.
Title: Consumer Protection - Agricultural Equipment Warranties

NarrowSubjects.Name: Agriculture -see also- Agritourism; Cannabis Prd; Farm; etc.
Equipment -see also- Charging; Med. Equip.; MV Equip; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: The bill establishes the Agricultural Equipment Warranty Enforcement Act, which requires consumers of self-propelled farming equipment to report defects in writing to manufacturers or dealers. It mandates that nonconformities be corrected within 30 days and provides consumers the right to a replacement or refund if the equipment remains defective after multiple repair attempts or is out of service for a cumulative total of 30 days during a season of use. Violations are designated as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
stakeholders: Consumers (including farmers) purchasing new agricultural equipment, as well as manufacturers, factory branches, and authorized dealers of such equipment.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to have no material impact on State or local finances or operations. The Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division can implement the bill using existing resources. While no specific appropriation is provided, violations are subject to existing civil and criminal penalties under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, and courts may award up to $5,000 in damages to consumers if a manufacturer is found to have acted in bad faith.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill defines violations of the Agricultural Equipment Warranty Enforcement Act as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, which the Office of the Attorney General is primary responsible for enforcing.

The bill focuses exclusively on 'agricultural equipment' used in the business of farming. This is directly relevant to the Department's mission to support the economic viability of the farming sector and provide consumer confidence in agricultural services.

The bill creates a new civil cause of action for consumers to enforce warranty claims and allows for courts to award damages for bad faith, which impacts the operations of the Maryland Judicial Branch.

The bill applies to self-propelled vehicles and specifically mentions the refund of license and registration fees, which are administered and collected by the MVA. The bill also references definitions within the Transportation Article.

As an agency that adjudicates contested cases involving state regulatory enforcement, OAH may be involved in administrative hearings arising from consumer protection enforcement actions under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.

Agricultural equipment is a critical asset for the economies of Maryland's rural counties. The Council advocates for interests that improve the quality of life and economic development for farmers and rural residents.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies (such as MDA and OAG) that will be involved in implementing or enforcing this policy, and the Governor is responsible for signing the legislation.

responsible_party: Maryland Department of Natural Resources
stakeholders: Shellfish aquaculture harvester permit holders, registration card holders, and shellfish aquaculture leaseholders.

Revenues are not materially affected, and there is no fiscal impact on local governments or small businesses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly provides for judicial review of the Department of Natural Resources' final decisions regarding the suspension or revocation of permits, which involves the state's judicial system managed by the AOC.
The bill codifies a violation of the Maryland Department of Health's Vibrio Parahaemolyticus Control Plan as specific grounds for the suspension or revocation of a shellfish aquaculture permit.

As the primary agency for managing shellfish aquaculture, DNR is responsible for issuing permits, holding administrative hearings, enforcing suspensions and revocations, and managing the lease transfer process established by the bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Natural Resources and the Department of Health and would represent the state in any judicial reviews of the administrative decisions made under this bill.

bill_summary: This bill establishes and standardizes criminal history records check (CHRC) requirements for various health occupation boards in Maryland. It requires initial applicants, and in many cases individuals seeking license renewal or reinstatement, to submit fingerprints for state and national background checks performed by the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health health occupation boards and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Applicants and licensed health professionals under boards for acupuncture, dental examiners, dietetic practice, environmental health, morticians, nursing, optometry, pharmacy, physical therapy, podiatry, psychology, and residential child care.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services (DPSCS) will experience an indeterminate increase in general fund revenues and expenditures starting in FY 2028 due to an estimated 52,584 additional background checks. Based on an $18 fee per check, DPSCS revenues could increase by up to $946,512. The various health occupation boards are expected to implement the administrative changes using existing budgeted resources. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the Department of Health and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, which are the primary agencies responsible for implementing this bill. The Governor also appoints members to the various health occupation boards affected by the legislation.

As the state's principal tax collector and chief financial officer, the Comptroller's office may be involved in the management of revenues generated from the criminal history records check fees paid by applicants, which are projected to increase general fund revenues.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the specific health occupation boards regarding the implementation of the new criminal history records check requirements, confidentiality of records, and handling of contested cases.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees state budget execution and personnel. The fiscal note indicates that the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services may require additional staff and general fund expenditures to handle the increased workload of processing up to 52,000 additional background checks.

The Maryland Department of Health is highly relevant as it houses the 12 specific health occupation boards (e.g., Dental, Pharmacy, Nursing) for which the bill establishes or alters criminal history records check requirements for licensing and certification.

The bill impacts the State Board for Certification of Residential Child Care Program Professionals, who work in programs and facilities often regulated or utilized by the Department of Human Services for children in state care.

The bill impacts the certification requirements for Residential Child Care Program Professionals, who are essential staff in residential facilities that may house youth under the supervision of the Department of Juvenile Services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency is a primary implementer of the bill, as the Criminal Justice Information System (CJIS) Central Repository is housed within DPSCS and is responsible for conducting the state and national criminal history records checks mandated for health occupations.

The Maryland State Police are part of the broader state law enforcement and criminal record infrastructure that supports the background check and fingerprinting processes utilized by the CJIS Central Repository.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly regulates the administrative and regulatory procedures of 12 separate health occupation boards (e.g., Board of Acupuncture, Board of Dental Examiners), which fall under this collective category of executive bodies.

The Office of Administrative Hearings may be required to adjudicate contested cases where applicants or licensees challenge the results of their criminal history records checks or the subsequent licensing decisions made by the health boards.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Secretary of Budget and Management to set higher pay scales for Chief Financial Officers (CFOs) and Chief Information Officers (CIOs) in large Executive Branch units to improve recruitment and retention. It establishes minimum qualifications for CFO positions, requires these units to report specific financial data to the Office of the Comptroller, and expands documentation and reporting requirements for state units that waive liquidated damages on procurement contracts regardless of contract value.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Budget and Management
stakeholders: Chief Financial Officers and Chief Information Officers in large Executive Branch units, state agencies, the Board of Public Works, and state procurement contractors.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general and special fund expenditures may increase beginning in fiscal 2027 due to potential salary increases for CFO and CIO positions. The fiscal 2027 budget includes $4,000,000 in the Dedicated Purpose Account to strengthen fiscal leadership capacity, which may be used for this purpose. The bill's provisions regarding liquidated damages are procedural and have no direct fiscal impact, and there is no impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor oversees the executive branch and signs the legislation. The bill impacts the administrative structure and personnel management (CFO/CIO pay scales) for which the Governor's Office coordinates policy.

The bill explicitly requires Chief Financial Officers of specified units to provide financial information, federal expenditure data, and attestation letters to the Office of the Comptroller for the preparation of the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report.

The State Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works, which receives documentation regarding decisions not to pursue liquidated damages. The Treasurer also has a role in managing state funds and fiscal oversight.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding procurement contracts and liquidated damages. Procurement officers typically consult with the OAG when deciding whether to include or enforce liquidated damages clauses.
DBM is the primary implementing agency. The Secretary of DBM is authorized to set pay scales for CFO and CIO positions, establish minimum qualifications for CFOs, and adopt related regulations.

MSDE is specifically identified in the fiscal note as one of the agencies likely to meet the $1.75 billion funding threshold, meaning its CFO position will be subject to the bill's pay scale and reporting requirements.
As a central procurement authority, DGS is directly impacted by the bill's new documentation and approval requirements for liquidated damages in procurement contracts.
MDH is identified as one of the high-funding agencies ($1.75B+) whose CFO position will be subject to the new pay scale authority and financial reporting mandates.
DHS is identified as an affected high-funding agency whose CFO position will be subject to the bill's personnel and reporting requirements.

The bill establishes pay scale and recruitment authority for Chief Information Officers (CIOs) within the executive branch, which aligns with DoIT's mission to manage the state's IT strategy and personnel.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is identified as a high-funding agency impacted by the bill's provisions regarding CFO qualifications, pay scales, and fiscal reporting.
MDOT is identified as a high-funding agency impacted by the bill's provisions regarding CFO qualifications, pay scales, and fiscal reporting.
The bill requires state units to provide documentation to the Board of Public Works when they intend not to pursue liquidated damages for a contract breach.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the September 30 deadline for Baltimore City Class A beer and light wine or beer, wine, and liquor license holders to pay the $120 supplementary fee for Sunday sales between Thanksgiving and New Year's Day. It also moves the annual deadline for these license holders to provide proof of paid personal property taxes to the Board of Liquor License Commissioners from October 30 to March 30.
responsible_party: Baltimore City Board of Liquor License Commissioners
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverages license holders in Baltimore City, specifically Class A beer and light wine and Class A beer, wine, and liquor licensees.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no effect on State finances and is not expected to materially affect Baltimore City finances or operations. Small business impact is minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is responsible for overseeing the executive branch and signing or vetoing legislation passed by the General Assembly. This bill requires the Governor's signature to become law and involves state-level regulation of alcoholic beverages through the Annotated Code of Maryland.

The Comptroller is the state's principal tax collector and regulates the alcohol industry. The bill requires license holders to present proof that personal property taxes due to the State have been paid and amends administrative procedures for alcoholic beverage licensing fees.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the State and provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies. They may be required to interpret the legal implications of the revisions to the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article.

County revenues are not affected.

As the office responsible for vetting and recommending candidates for gubernatorial appointments, this agency is directly affected by the removal of the Governor's power to fill vacancies on this specific board.

The bill makes structural, compensation, and operational changes to the Somerset County Board of Education, which is a local component of the state's public education system overseen by the Maryland State Department of Education.
