bill_summary: This bill establishes a dedicated funding stream for public charter school facilities in Maryland, requiring the Interagency Commission on School Construction to distribute funds directly to charter schools for capital improvements, debt service, or rent and lease payments. To qualify for funding, a charter school must have had an unqualified audit in the previous fiscal year and cannot concurrently receive certain other state capital funding for the same facility. Beginning in fiscal year 2028, the Governor must include a mandated appropriation in the annual budget calculated by multiplying the previous year's total public charter school enrollment by $200.
responsible_party: Interagency Commission on School Construction
stakeholders: Public charter schools and their students, and the Interagency Commission on School Construction.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures increase by $116,835 in fiscal 2027 for administrative staffing and by approximately $5,200,000 annually beginning in fiscal 2028 to meet the bill's mandated appropriation of $200 per pupil. Federal fund revenues may increase if this program allows the State to qualify for competitive federal Charter Schools Program grants. Local school systems are not expected to see a fiscal impact as funds are paid directly to the charter schools.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill identifies the IAC as the primary agency responsible for distributing funds to public charter schools, adopting regulations for the program, and receiving mandatory status reports from the schools.

DBM is responsible for the state's budget development and must manage the mandated $200 per-pupil appropriation. The fiscal note also indicates that DBM will oversee the personnel increase required for the IAC to manage this new grant program.
MSDE provides the aggregate student enrollment data used to calculate the mandatory funding amount and oversees the Maryland Public Charter School Program which this bill directly impacts.
The bill mandates that the Governor include a specific per-pupil appropriation in the annual budget bill for charter school facilities starting in fiscal year 2028.

As the body that oversees significant state expenditures and the Public School Construction Program (PSCP), the Board of Public Works has ultimate oversight over the capital improvement funds mentioned in the bill.

The OAG will be required to provide legal counsel to the IAC for the creation of new regulations and to ensure that direct payments to charter schools comply with state constitutional and statutory requirements.
As the state's chief financial officer and a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller is involved in the oversight and processing of state payments to charter schools.
The Treasurer manages state funds and serves on the Board of Public Works, which oversees the school construction funding and capital projects affected by the bill's provisions.
The OAH could be called upon to adjudicate disputes if a charter school's eligibility for funding is contested, specifically regarding the audit requirements or project status reporting.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to establish and maintain a centralized caregiver resource webpage to support various types of caregivers in the state. The webpage must provide plain-language, easily accessible information and links to resources concerning children with disabilities, adults with chronic illness or behavioral health needs, and older adults, as well as health and wellness, financial assistance, and safety planning for caregivers.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Caregivers in Maryland, including parents of children with disabilities, individuals caring for family members with chronic illnesses or functional limitations, and minor or dependent caregivers.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the Maryland Department of Health can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. There is no impact on State revenues or local governmental operations and finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, the Maryland Department of Health is responsible for developing, hosting, and maintaining the centralized caregiver resource webpage, and coordinating with other state entities as required by the bill.

The bill explicitly requires the Maryland Department of Health to coordinate with the Department of Aging in the development of the webpage. The agency also manages related resources like the Maryland Access Point for long-term services and supports for older adults and their caregivers.

The bill explicitly names the State Department of Education as a coordinating partner for the webpage's development, specifically regarding information and school-based supports for children with disabilities and special health care needs.

The department is responsible for improving service delivery to Maryland residents with disabilities and their families. The bill's focus on resources for caregivers of individuals with disabilities directly aligns with this agency's mission and coordination role.

The fiscal note indicates that the Department of Human Services staffs the Maryland Commission on Caregiving, which is responsible for coordinating statewide planning and handbooks for family caregiver support services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This category includes the Maryland Commission on Caregiving, which is specifically mentioned in the fiscal note as the entity responsible for coordinating statewide caregiver support and distributing handbooks for current services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note highlights this agency as a coordinator for the Maryland Access Point (MAP) program. The bill's mandate for caregiver resources for individuals with functional limitations includes the population served by this office.

This agency provides support services to deaf and hard-of-hearing students and their families. It is a relevant resource for the 'educational and school-based supports' section of the caregiver webpage mandated by the bill.

The agency's focus on the well-being of Maryland's children and families, particularly those in underinvested communities, overlaps with the bill's requirement to provide resources for caregivers of children with disabilities and special health care needs.

DoIT is responsible for the state's IT strategy and infrastructure. The bill's requirements for a centralized webpage and specific considerations for data security and privacy when using technology to support caregiving fall under DoIT's technical oversight.

The agency oversees the Maryland State Library for the Blind and Print Disabled, which serves individuals with functional limitations and their caregivers, making it a relevant resource for the mandated webpage.

Caregivers for veterans with disabilities or chronic illnesses are included in the bill's broad definition of caregivers, making this agency a relevant partner for resource links and program information.

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland municipalities to submit candidate qualifications, election dates, candidate lists, and voting procedure information to the State Board of Elections (SBE) for publication on the board's website. Municipalities using ranked-choice voting are also required to submit their tabulation regulations. The SBE must publish this information immediately upon receipt to ensure public access to municipal election details.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections
stakeholders: Maryland municipalities, candidates for municipal office, and voters in municipal elections.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland State Board of Elections can implement the bill's requirements using existing resources, resulting in no State fiscal impact. Similarly, the bill is not expected to materially affect local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the State Board of Elections to receive candidate qualifications, candidate lists, and voting procedures from municipalities and requires the Board to publish this information on its website immediately upon receipt.

As the chief legal officer for state agencies, the Office of the Attorney General would provide legal counsel to the State Board of Elections regarding the implementation of these new reporting requirements and the publication of municipal regulations for ranked-choice voting.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Suitland Development Authority in Prince George’s County to revitalize and develop neighborhoods along the Suitland Road and Silver Hill Road corridor. The Authority is authorized to coordinate with residents to create a comprehensive revitalization plan, acquire and manage property, provide loans and grants, and oversee economic, housing, and transportation projects to promote community growth and safety.
responsible_party: Prince George's County Suitland Development Authority
stakeholders: Residents and commercial property owners in the Suitland Road and Silver Hill Road corridor of Prince George's County.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note assumes State general fund expenditures will increase by at least $10,000,000 annually from FY 2027 through 2035 to ensure the Authority is viable, with a mandated annual appropriation of $500,000 starting in FY 2028. The Authority is required to be self-sustaining starting in FY 2036. Prince George's County finances may be impacted by potential local funding contributions and changes in real property tax revenues resulting from development and tax exemptions provided by the bill.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates the Suitland Development Authority as a state instrumentality and mandates that the Governor include a $500,000 annual appropriation in the state budget for the Authority. The Governor is also responsible for the overall execution of laws relating to this new executive-branch entity.

The Comptroller is explicitly required by the bill to account for the Suitland Development Authority Fund and is responsible for managing the state's tax laws, which include the specific sales and use tax and recordation tax exemptions granted to the Authority.
The bill requires the State Treasurer to hold the Suitland Development Authority Fund separately and to invest the money of the Fund in the same manner as other State money.

As the chief legal officer for the State, the OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to the newly established Suitland Development Authority and representing it in its capacity as an instrumentality of the State.

DBM is the principal agency for developing the state budget and managing personnel. Although the Authority is exempt from certain DBM oversight, the department must manage the mandated $500,000 appropriation and potential multi-million dollar fiscal impacts noted in the fiscal note.

The Secretary of Commerce (or a designee) is a mandated member of the Authority's Board of Directors. The agency's mission of economic development and job attraction is a core purpose of the new Authority.

The Secretary of Housing and Community Development (or a designee) is a mandated member of the Authority's Board of Directors. The Authority's focus on neighborhood revitalization, housing development, and community improvement directly aligns with DHCD's core mission.

The Secretary of Transportation (or a designee) is a mandated member of the Authority's Board of Directors. The Authority's mission specifically includes transportation planning for motor vehicles and pedestrians within the revitalization area.

The Authority is subject to State Finance and Procurement Article Title 12, Subtitle 4, which requires exempt units to submit their written procurement policies and procedures to the Board of Public Works for review.

The Executive Director of the Maryland Economic Development Corporation (MEDCO) is a mandated member of the Authority's Board of Directors, providing a direct link between the state's primary economic development instrumentality and this new local authority.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly subjects the Authority to Title 14, Subtitle 3 of the State Finance and Procurement Article regarding Minority Business Enterprise (MBE) participation, which this office monitors and implements across state agencies.
The bill explicitly subjects the Authority's board members, officers, and employees to the Maryland Public Ethics Law, which is administered and enforced by this commission.

As a new state instrumentality with mandated funding and a dedicated special fund, the Authority will be subject to periodic fiscal compliance and performance audits by the OLA to ensure accountability and efficiency.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Circuit Administrative Judge of the Fourth Circuit to establish a Truancy Reduction Pilot Program in the juvenile court in Washington County.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Circuit Administrative Judge of the Fourth Circuit to establish a Truancy Reduction Pilot Program within the juvenile court of Washington County to address habitual truancy through specialized court-ordered interventions and services.
responsible_party: Circuit Administrative Judge of the Fourth Circuit
stakeholders: Habitually truant juveniles in Washington County, their parents or legal guardians, the Washington County school system, and the juvenile court system.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $155,000 annually for the Judiciary to provide grant funding for the program. Washington County will see a corresponding increase of $155,000 in local grant revenues and expenditures for program implementation. The Office of the Public Defender may face increased caseloads, although the exact fiscal impact on that agency is currently indeterminate.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill authorizes the Circuit Administrative Judge to establish the Truancy Reduction Pilot Program. The Administrative Office of the Courts, specifically the Office of Problem-Solving Courts, provides the $155,000 annual grant funding and operational support for such programs within the Judiciary.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note explicitly mentions a potential operational impact on the Office of the Public Defender, noting that truancy programs generate additional cases for parents and juveniles, potentially requiring significant additional attorney and support resources.

Truancy reduction is fundamentally an educational compliance matter under the Education Article. School officials are responsible for filing the petitions that initiate the program's court proceedings, and local school board staff often provide essential support services.

Habitually truant children are often designated as Children in Need of Supervision (CINS), which falls under the jurisdiction of the juvenile court. The Department of Juvenile Services manages and supervises youth within this system.
As the agency responsible for developing the state's budget and supervising budget execution, DBM is relevant because the program requires a dedicated annual general fund expenditure of $155,000.

The Governor's Office for Children is tasked with improving access to education and coordinating support networks for Maryland's children. A truancy reduction program aligns directly with their mission to improve well-being and educational outcomes.
The Governor oversees the executive branch, proposes the annual state budget (which must include funding for this pilot), and signs the legislation into law.

bill_summary: This bill expands the definition of a 'qualified property' under the Appraisal Gap From Historic Redlining Financial Assistance Program. responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
stakeholders: Affordable housing developers and individuals purchasing owner-occupied residential properties in historically redlined or urban renewal neighborhoods.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill does not materially affect State or local government operations or finances. The expansion of the definition of 'qualified property' increases the number of properties eligible for the program but does not change existing funding levels or mandated expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, DHCD is responsible for administering the Appraisal Gap From Historic Redlining Financial Assistance Program and is specifically tasked by the bill with establishing criteria to identify neighborhoods that have been historically redlined or undergone urban renewal.

The bill references 'sustainable communities,' a designation that involves the state's planning visions and coordination between agencies including the Department of Planning to promote community revitalization and sustainable growth.

The bill directly addresses enhancing economic mobility and supporting underinvested communities by mitigating historical redlining, which aligns with the Innovation Team's mandate to pilot novel initiatives for these specific goals.
The program's goal of improving economic opportunities and addressing historical disinvestment in neighborhoods supports the office's mission to enhance the well-being of families and reduce poverty.
The OAG provides legal counsel to DHCD and would be involved in the development of regulations and the legal interpretation of the newly established criteria for 'qualified properties.'
This multi-agency initiative coordinates community revitalization and sustainable development efforts, which are central to the definitions and objectives of the Appraisal Gap program.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the budget for DHCD and the execution of funding for the financial assistance program, even if the bill's fiscal impact is determined to be minimal.
The Governor oversees the executive branch, including DHCD, and coordinates the broader policy initiatives related to housing equity and urban renewal that this bill addresses.

The bill addresses the effects of historical redlining, a form of housing discrimination; while the bill is programmatic rather than enforcement-based, it aligns with the Commission's interest in fair housing and addressing historical inequities.

Synopsis: Requiring, beginning in 2026, the Maryland Department of Health to conduct the in-State cost-of-dispensing survey at least every 3 years;  and requiring the Department to report the results of the survey to the General Assembly by December 1 in each year the survey is required.
Title: Medical Assistance Programs - Drug Dispensing - Cost-of-Dispensing Survey

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to conduct an in-State cost-of-dispensing survey for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program at least once every three years, beginning in 2026. The department is also required to report the results of each survey to the General Assembly by December 1 of the year it is conducted.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Maryland Department of Health, retail pharmacy providers, and the Maryland General Assembly.
fiscal_impact_summary: State Medicaid expenditures increase by $81,000 in FY 2027, FY 2030, and every three years thereafter to conduct the cost-of-dispensing survey. This cost is split equally between general funds ($40,500) and federal funds ($40,500), with federal fund revenues increasing accordingly. The Maryland Department of Health can report the survey results using existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary agency responsible for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) and is specifically mandated by the bill to conduct the in-State cost-of-dispensing survey every three years and report the results to the General Assembly.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for state budget development and supervising budget execution. As the bill creates a recurring fiscal impact on general and federal funds for Medicaid expenditures ($81,000 every three years), the department will oversee the fiscal planning for these costs.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the Department of Health and is responsible for proposing the state budget, which must now account for the recurring costs of the mandated cost-of-dispensing surveys.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for all state agencies, including the Department of Health, and would provide legal counsel regarding the implementation of the survey and compliance with federal and state Medicaid regulations.

Synopsis: Establishing the Maryland's Future Board under the Department of Commerce to develop, evaluate, and revise a visionary plan for the future of Maryland by January 1, 2027; requiring the Board to make recommendations for projects based on the plan to the Governor and the General Assembly by August 1, 2027 and each August 1 thereafter; establishing the Maryland's Future Fund; and requiring the Comptroller to study economic growth trends for certain industries and report to the General Assembly by December 1, 2026.
Title: Economic Development - Maryland's Future Board - Establishment

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland’s Future Board within the Department of Commerce to develop, evaluate, and revise a long-term visionary plan for the state's economic future, focusing on emerging trends such as artificial intelligence, robotics, and advanced manufacturing. It also creates the Maryland’s Future Fund, a special nonlapsing fund to finance projects recommended by the Board, and requires the Comptroller to study and report on Maryland's economic growth trends and competitive industries.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Commerce
stakeholders: Maryland residents, entrepreneurs, academic institutions, labor organizations, business leaders, and nonprofit organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State general fund expenditures will increase by $1,700,000 in FY 2027, which includes $200,000 for the Comptroller’s economic study and $1,500,000 for the Maryland’s Future Fund and Board administration. Ongoing general fund expenditures will be required through FY 2031 for board operations and to capitalize the Maryland’s Future Fund for project execution, which could potentially require at least several million dollars annually starting in FY 2029. Local governments are not directly affected but may benefit from future visionary projects.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Maryland’s Future Board within the Department of Commerce and designates the Department as the administrator of the newly created Maryland’s Future Fund.

The Comptroller (or a designee) is a mandated member of the Board and is explicitly required by the bill to conduct a study on economic growth trends and identify growth needs in competitive industries.
The Governor appoints three members to the Board and is the primary recipient of the visionary plan and project recommendations designed to advance the state’s socioeconomic wellbeing.
The State Treasurer is responsible for holding the Maryland’s Future Fund separately and investing its money, with interest earnings being credited back to the fund.

As the agency responsible for the state's budget development, DBM is impacted by the Board's recommendations for projects which specifically include allocations in the state's operating and capital budgets.

The Board's mission to identify and test novel initiatives related to economic mobility and industry disruptive technologies aligns closely with the Innovation Team's role as a solution incubator for the Governor's top priorities.

The bill focuses on future industry trends like robotics and AI, which directly intersects with the GWDB's responsibility for developing innovative workforce solutions and setting the statewide vision for workforce development.
The Board is required to include leaders from labor organizations, and the visionary plan covers areas such as advanced technology workforce training and job replacement due to AI.
The Board's membership includes leaders from higher education and academia to help develop strategies for a future economic landscape that attracts residents who want to learn in Maryland.

GOPI oversees the implementation of the State Comprehensive Plan and aligns agency activities with Governor priorities; the board's visionary plan for future economic strength will require interagency alignment.

Synopsis: Repealing certain prohibitions on a transfer to different premises or a conversion to a different class of license that apply to certain alcoholic beverages licenses issued, reissued, or transferred by the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore County; and requiring certain Class B beer, wine, and liquor licenses in existence on a certain date to be converted into certain Class B hotel and restaurant licenses before a certain date.
Title: Baltimore County - Alcoholic Beverages Licenses - Transfers and Conversions
bill_summary: This bill repeals prohibitions on the transfer of alcoholic beverages licenses to different premises or their conversion to different classes in Baltimore County. It specifically requires certain Class B licenses (including those in the Towson Commercial Revitalization District, Hunt Valley, and Metro Center at Owings Mills) to be converted into standard Class B hotel and restaurant licenses by July 1, 2026, and removes restrictions on moving licenses between election districts or reissuing revoked licenses.
responsible_party: Baltimore County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage license holders in Baltimore County, particularly those in specific commercial districts like Towson and Hunt Valley, and the Baltimore County Board of License Commissioners.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not expected to materially affect Baltimore County finances or operations, and the impact on small businesses is estimated to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the principal state agency responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and enforcing related tax laws. This bill directly amends the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article to repeal prohibitions on license transfers and require the conversion of specific license classes in Baltimore County, which impacts the regulatory and oversight framework managed by the Comptroller's office.

Synopsis: Repealing the authority of the State Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists to issue a temporary telehealth license; and exempting certain State licensure requirements for certain individuals who are licensed in another state and who provide counseling through telehealth to clients in the State.
Title: Clinical Professional Counseling - Out-of-State Providers - Use of Telehealth for Continuity of Care

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits
Mental and Behavioral Health -see also- Aut; Cogn; Dev; etc.

bill_summary: The bill repeals the authority of the State Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists to issue temporary telehealth licenses and instead creates exemptions from state licensure requirements for out-of-state clinical professional counselors and social workers. These providers may provide telehealth services for up to six months to ensure continuity of care for clients who have recently relocated or returned to Maryland, provided a prior therapeutic relationship existed outside the state.
responsible_party: State Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists and the State Board of Social Work Examiners
stakeholders: Out-of-state licensed clinical professional counselors, licensed social workers, and clients who relocate to or return to Maryland while receiving mental health or social work services.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State Board revenues and expenditures are not materially affected by the bill. There is no impact on local government or small businesses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) as it amends the Health Occupations Article, specifically Title 17 (Professional Counselors and Therapists) and Title 19 (Social Workers). MDH oversees the regulatory boards responsible for licensing these professionals and implementing the new telehealth continuity of care exemptions.

The bill repeals Section 17-304.2, which specifically governed temporary telehealth licenses for out-of-state students attending institutions of higher education in Maryland. The Commission coordinates policy for these institutions and the students affected by this shift to a broader continuity of care model.

DHS is the state's primary employer and coordinator of social work services. Changes to the Social Work (Title 19) licensing requirements and exemptions for out-of-state providers through telehealth affect the landscape of available social service professionals and the standards of practice within the state.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the health occupation boards within MDH. They will be responsible for advising on the implementation of the new licensure exemptions and ensuring that regulations regarding out-of-state providers comply with the new statutory framework.

USM institutions operate campus counseling centers. The bill's repeal of the temporary telehealth license specifically intended for students, replacing it with a general 6-month continuity of care exemption, directly impacts how campus health services coordinate mental health care for incoming out-of-state students.

As a public university, Morgan State provides counseling services to its students. The changes to telehealth licensing laws for out-of-state providers affect how the university manages mental health care for students who have established therapeutic relationships before moving to Baltimore.

As a state agency and public college, SMCM is affected by the repeal of the student-specific temporary telehealth license and the transition to a general continuity of care exemption for out-of-state counselors and social workers.

DBM oversees the fiscal and personnel impacts of legislation. While the fiscal note indicates no material impact, the change in licensing structures and potential effects on board revenues or expenditures fall under DBM's monitoring responsibilities.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and MDH. This bill requires gubernatorial approval and aligns with policy initiatives related to healthcare access and telehealth regulation.

The Department of Disabilities is interested in the delivery of services via telehealth, which is often a critical access point for individuals with disabilities. Changes to out-of-state provider regulations for mental health and social work can impact service accessibility for this population.

Veterans and military families frequently relocate. This bill provides a 6-month window of continuity for mental health care through telehealth for individuals moving into Maryland, which is a significant issue for military-connected populations transitioning to the state.

DJS manages and treats youth in the juvenile justice system, often employing or contracting with clinical professional counselors and social workers. Changes to licensing exemptions for these professions are relevant to the agency's mental health service delivery standards.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS utilizes clinical professional counselors and social workers for the rehabilitation of justice-involved individuals. Regulation of these professions, including out-of-state practice via telehealth, is relevant to the department's medical and rehabilitative services.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases for state agencies, including the health occupation boards. If disputes arise regarding an individual's eligibility for the new licensure exemptions or disciplinary actions related to telehealth practice, OAH would likely handle the administrative appeals.

Synopsis: Prohibiting the Department of Human Services from denying an application or reducing or terminating temporary cash assistance from an individual if the individual has good cause or an adequate reason for noncooperation with child support; defining "good cause" as circumstances in which cooperation with child support may be against the best interest of the child; requiring the Family Investment Program to determine that there is good cause for noncooperation with child support using certain criteria; etc.
Title: Family Investment Program - Temporary Cash Assistance - Good Cause and Adequate Reason Exceptions

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Public Benefits -see also- Housing; MedAsst;  SupplNutrAsstP

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the Department of Human Services from denying, reducing, or terminating Temporary Cash Assistance (TCA) for individuals who have 'good cause' or 'adequate reasons' for not cooperating with child support requirements. It establishes specific criteria for these exceptions—such as risks of harm, cases of incest or rape, or pending adoptions—and requires the department to notify applicants of their right to claim them. The bill also simplifies the application process by allowing oral statements to prove good cause and prohibiting the requirement of third-party verification or notarized documents.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Applicants for and recipients of Temporary Cash Assistance (TCA), their children, and the staff of the Family Investment Program and Child Support Administration.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the Department of Human Services can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. There is no projected impact on State revenues or local governmental finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency overseeing the Family Investment Program (FIP) and the Child Support Administration (CSA), DHS is responsible for implementing the new criteria for 'good cause' and 'adequate reason' exceptions and managing the resulting impacts on Temporary Cash Assistance (TCA) eligibility and distribution.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases involving state agencies; changes to TCA eligibility, including new criteria for noncooperation exceptions, directly affect the administrative appeals process for residents whose benefits are denied, reduced, or terminated.

The bill's focus on Temporary Cash Assistance and preventing the reduction of benefits for families aligns with the GOC's specific mission to coordinate statewide efforts to reduce child poverty and improve outcomes for vulnerable children.
The Innovation Team is specifically charged with piloting initiatives to address child poverty and enhance economic mobility; this bill's reform of the TCA system directly supports these goals.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Human Services and would likely assist in the development of regulations and legal interpretations of the new 'good cause' and 'adequate reason' criteria.
DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for the state's budget and would oversee the fiscal implications of changes to the Temporary Cash Assistance program managed by DHS.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates major policy initiatives, including the SERVE Act and poverty reduction strategies that this bill supports.

GOPI utilizes performance metrics to oversee the implementation of the state's priorities; reducing child poverty is a top priority, making the performance of the TCA program relevant to their oversight role.

Synopsis: Requiring the State Highway Administration to prioritize certain funding for the construction and reconstruction of sidewalks and bicycle pathways to sidewalks and bicycle pathways that are, or are adjacent to highways that are, subject to a complete streets policy or another similar Vision Zero program; requiring a local government to request certain funding from the Department of Transportation; and authorizing certain State funding for the construction or reconstruction of sidewalks or bicycle pathways.
Title: Highways - Sidewalks and Bicycle Pathways - Construction and Reconstruction (The Honorable Anne Healey Pedestrian Safety Act of 2026)

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.

bill_summary: The bill requires the State Highway Administration to prioritize funding for sidewalk and bicycle pathway projects located near highways subject to complete streets or Vision Zero safety programs. It mandates that local governments request such funding through annual priority letters and allows for varying levels of State cost-sharing, including full State funding for certain projects in sustainable communities or areas with significant safety risks.
responsible_party: State Highway Administration
stakeholders: Local governments, pedestrians, bicyclists, and the Maryland Department of Transportation
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not affect total Transportation Trust Fund expenditures but may result in a different prioritization of sidewalk and bicycle pathway projects starting as early as fiscal 2027. Local government finances may be affected as some jurisdictions receive more or less funding than under current law; additionally, the State Highway Administration may fully fund right-of-way acquisition costs for certain projects with substantial safety risks. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the impact depends on future project selections.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the state budget and the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF). The bill alters how funds within the TTF are prioritized and modifies state-local cost-sharing ratios for infrastructure projects.
The bill provides for full state funding of sidewalks and bicycle pathways within 'sustainable communities,' a designation defined and managed by the Department of Housing and Community Development.

The bill's cost-sharing requirements for infrastructure projects are based on whether a project is located within a 'priority funding area,' which is a geographic designation managed and coordinated by the Department of Planning.

MDOT is the parent agency of the State Highway Administration. The bill requires local governments to submit project requests in annual priority letters for MDOT's consideration in the Consolidated Transportation Program (CTP).

The bill mandates that the State Highway Administration prioritize projects based on 'Vision Zero' and 'Complete Streets' programs, which are key executive policy initiatives coordinated through the Governor's Office.

SHA is the primary agency responsible for the construction and reconstruction of sidewalks and bicycle pathways on state highways. The bill specifically directs SHA's funding prioritization and project evaluation criteria.

Synopsis: Authorizing and empowering the County Commissioners of Calvert County, from time to time, to borrow not more than $80,957,080 to finance the construction, improvement, or development of certain public buildings, roads, and facilities in Calvert County, and to effect such borrowing by the issuance and sale at public or private sale of its general obligation bonds in like par amount; etc.
Title: Calvert County - Public Facilities Bonds

Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Calvert County Commissioners to borrow up to $80,957,080 through the issuance of general obligation bonds to finance the construction, improvement, or development of various public facilities, including public buildings, roads, and storm drainage systems.
responsible_party: County Commissioners of Calvert County
stakeholders: Residents and taxpayers of Calvert County, Calvert County Government, and users of local public facilities such as schools and senior centers.
fiscal_impact_summary: Calvert County will receive up to $80,957,080 in bond proceeds for capital projects. The fiscal note estimates that annual debt service expenditures will increase by approximately $6,300,000 (roughly $4.6 million for 15-year bonds and $1.7 million for 25-year bonds). The bill has no impact on Maryland State finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor is responsible for signing the bill into law, which provides the necessary legislative authorization for Calvert County to borrow funds and issue general obligation bonds for public facilities.

The bill explicitly exempts the authorized bonds and the interest derived from them from all Maryland state and local taxation, which is relevant to the Comptroller's role as the state's principal tax collector and revenue administrator.

The bond proceeds are specifically intended to fund renovations at the Calvert Pines Senior Center, which aligns with the department's mission to oversee programs and facilities that improve the quality of life for older adults.

The bill authorizes funding for several public school projects, including Northern Middle School and Southern Middle School, which are part of the state's public education system overseen by the department.

The bond authority includes $1.5 million for local health department facilities, which are regulated and overseen by the Maryland Department of Health as part of the state's public health infrastructure.

A significant portion of the bond request (over $26 million) is allocated for wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) upgrades, sewer collection, and landfill projects, all of which fall under the environmental and water quality regulatory authority of the Department of the Environment.

The bill authorizes funding for county road paving and construction projects, including the Prince Frederick Loop Road and Boyd's Turn Road, which connect to the broader state transportation network managed by MDOT.

The bill facilitates the funding and execution of public school capital improvement projects, such as Northern and Southern Middle Schools, which are specifically overseen by the Commission to ensure facility sufficiency.

Synopsis: Altering the salaries of the County Commissioners of Calvert County, the president and members of the Calvert County Board of Education, and the County Treasurer of Calvert County; repealing a provision that the salary of State's Attorneys shall take effect at the beginning of the elected term of office and may not increase during the term of office; altering certain retirement benefits for the County Treasurer of Calvert County; providing that the Act does not apply to the salary or compensation of certain incumbent officials; etc.
Title: Calvert County - County Officials and Board of Education - Salaries and Benefits

Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc
Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates

bill_summary: This bill increases the annual salaries for several Calvert County officials, including the President and members of the Board of County Commissioners, the President and members of the County Board of Education, and the County Treasurer. It also adjusts retirement health benefits for County Commissioners and aligns the County Treasurer's pension benefits with those of other county employees. Additionally, it repeals a restriction that prevented the State's Attorney's salary from increasing during a term, allowing it to fluctuate with the salary of a circuit court judge.
responsible_party: Calvert County Board of County Commissioners
stakeholders: Calvert County Board of County Commissioners, Calvert County Board of Education, Calvert County Treasurer, Calvert County State's Attorney, and Calvert County taxpayers.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, Calvert County expenditures are expected to increase by approximately $52,300 in fiscal 2027 and by a minimum of $100,900 annually thereafter. Specifically, the costs are estimated at $106,800 in fiscal 2029 and $112,700 in fiscal 2030. These estimates account for salary increases but do not reflect potential additional costs from increased fringe benefits or specific pension benefit changes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation passed by the Maryland General Assembly, including this bill which impacts the salaries and benefits of local Calvert County officials.

The bill amends Section 3–303 of the Education Article to alter the annual compensation for the president and members of the Calvert County Board of Education. The Department of Education oversees the state's 24 local school systems, including their leadership structure and compensation standards.

The bill links the salary of the Calvert County State’s Attorney to the salary of a circuit court judge. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides financial and operational support to the judicial branch, including the management of judicial salaries used as the benchmark in this legislation.

The bill modifies the pension benefits for the Calvert County Treasurer to align with those of other county employees. Because many Maryland counties participate in the State Retirement and Pension System (SRPS) as participating governmental units, the SRA may be responsible for the administration and oversight of these modified benefits.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Governor and the General Assembly, reviewing legislation for constitutionality and legal sufficiency, particularly regarding local government authority and public official compensation.

Synopsis: Altering the violations of law with respect to which the Field Enforcement Division of the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission is authorized to issue a citation or charging document; prohibiting a retailer from distributing, selling, exposing for sale, or advertising for sale unauthorized consumable products; authorizing the Executive Director of the Commission to seize, confiscate, or destroy unauthorized consumable products and certain other products; etc.
Title: Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission - Unauthorized Consumable Products - Enforcement and Seizure

Tobacco and Nicotine -see also- Cigarettes; Smk&Vap

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission (ATCC) to regulate, seize, and destroy 'unauthorized consumable products,' which include tianeptine, non-compliant kratom, and phenibut. It prohibits retailers from selling or advertising these substances, especially to minors, and mandates that the Maryland Department of Health notify the ATCC of changes in the regulatory status of such products. Violations are classified as misdemeanors subject to fines and potential license revocation.
responsible_party: Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission (ATCC)
stakeholders: Retailers (including manufacturers, wholesalers, and stores), consumers of herbal or synthetic supplements, and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local fiscal impacts are expected to be minimal. The Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission and the Maryland Department of Health can implement the bill's provisions using existing budgeted resources. While the bill establishes criminal fines up to $5,000 and civil liability for retailers, these are not anticipated to have a material financial impact on State or local government operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is explicitly required to monitor the regulatory status of products like kratom, tianeptine, and phenibut and notify the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission of changes. The Secretary of Health also has the authority to designate certain consumable products for enforcement.

The bill authorizes the District Court to order the Comptroller to suspend or revoke specific licenses (such as tobacco or general business licenses) for retailers found in violation of the unauthorized consumable product prohibitions.

The bill grants new authority to the District Court to impose sanctions, order the seizure and destruction of products, and adjudicate misdemeanor criminal cases and civil liability claims arising from the bill's provisions.

The OAG serves as the primary legal counsel for the state agencies (MDH and ATCC) tasked with implementing these enforcement, seizure, and notification requirements, and would likely be involved in legal challenges or complex forfeiture proceedings.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive agencies involved (including MDH and the commissions within the executive branch) and the Governor must approve the designation of enforcement authorities and sign the bill into law.

DBM is responsible for the state budget and personnel management; the bill specifically references the Field Enforcement Division's ability to employ officers and employees as provided in the state budget.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes misdemeanor penalties that include potential imprisonment for up to 90 days, which would fall under the broader jurisdiction of state correctional and supervision systems if individuals are incarcerated.

Synopsis: Establishing in Carroll County a Class 1 distillery on-premises consumption permit; authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Carroll County to issue the permit to a holder of a Class 1 distillery license; authorizing the holder of a permit to sell, prepare, and serve certain food, nonalcoholic beverages, and alcoholic beverages for on-premises consumption; and authorizing the holder of the permit to use the licensed premises for events.
Title: Carroll County - Alcoholic Beverages - Class 1 Distillery On-Premises Consumption Permit

NarrowSubjects.Name: Alcoholic Beverages Manufacturing -see also- Breweries; etc.
Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Food -see also- Meat, Poultry, & Seafood; Milk; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a Class 1 distillery on-premises consumption permit in Carroll County, which allows the local Board of License Commissioners to grant permit holders the authority to sell, prepare, and serve food, nonalcoholic beverages, and specific distillery-produced alcoholic beverages for on-site consumption. It also allows distillery premises to be used for events, subject to approval from the Carroll County Health Department for food and beverage service.
responsible_party: Carroll County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Class 1 distillery license holders in Carroll County, the Carroll County Health Department, and the Carroll County Board of License Commissioners.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, Carroll County revenues may increase minimally beginning in fiscal 2027, depending on the permit fees established by the Board of License Commissioners. The bill is not expected to materially affect State finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the primary state official responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and issuing manufacturer's licenses. This bill directly references the Class 1 distillery license and its issuance by the Comptroller, and establishes a specific on-premises consumption permit for Carroll County relating to those licenses.

The bill explicitly requires that the authorization to sell, prepare, and serve food and non-alcoholic beverages at these distilleries be approved by the Carroll County Health Department, which operates under the oversight and policy guidance of the Maryland Department of Health.

The Governor is responsible for signing the bill into law and oversees the executive branch departments, such as the Comptroller and the Department of Health, that are involved in alcohol and food safety regulation.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for the state and its agencies, including providing counsel on the implementation of new licensing and permitting laws within the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article.

Synopsis: Decreasing from 3 years to 2 years the number of years for which an individual or the individual's parent or guardian must file taxes before the academic year for eligibility to receive an out-of-state tuition exemption at a public institution of higher education.
Title: Higher Education - Undocumented Students - Out-of-State Tuition Exemption Eligibility

NarrowSubjects.Name: Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.

bill_summary: This bill reduces the number of years (from three to two) that an individual or their parent or guardian must have filed Maryland income tax returns to qualify for an out-of-state tuition exemption at public institutions of higher education under the Maryland Dream Act. It also updates residency verification requirements for students to maintain their tuition status until they are awarded a degree.
responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission and the governing boards of public institutions of higher education
stakeholders: Undocumented students, their parents or legal guardians, Maryland public four-year universities, and Maryland community colleges
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures may increase minimally beginning in fiscal 2029 to accommodate additional full-time equivalent students in community college funding formulas, with estimated increases of $5,400 to $13,600 per student. The Maryland Higher Education Commission estimates an initial $20,000 increase in scholarship awards for the first cohort of newly eligible students, potentially rising to $80,000 after four years. Tuition revenues at public institutions may decrease minimally; for context, four-year institutions and community colleges reported revenue losses of $6,600,000 and $2,400,000 respectively in fiscal 2025 due to existing Dream Act exemptions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHEC is the primary regulatory and coordinating board for higher education in Maryland. It is responsible for overseeing the out-of-state tuition exemption policies, collecting annual reports from institutions regarding qualifying students, and administering state-funded scholarship programs (like the EEA and Promise scholarships) whose eligibility is directly impacted by changes in tuition status.

USM oversees 12 public institutions that must implement the revised eligibility criteria for tuition exemptions. These institutions will experience direct fiscal impacts through potential shifts in tuition revenue and adjustments to enrollment classifications.

As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State is directly responsible for applying the new tax-filing requirement to determine student eligibility for in-state tuition rates and may see associated impacts on tuition revenue.

As Maryland's public honors college, St. Mary's is directly affected by the change in tuition exemption criteria for undocumented students and the resulting impact on tuition revenue and student eligibility reporting.

The bill's eligibility criteria are based on Maryland income tax returns. The Comptroller's Office is the custodian of these records and plays a role in the verification process for students or parents/guardians seeking the tuition exemption.

DBM oversees the state budget and the funding formulas for higher education institutions (including the Cade and BCCC formulas). Changes in resident student enrollment counts resulting from this bill can affect state general fund expenditure requirements.

MLDS links student and workforce data from MHEC and other agencies. Changes in student residency and eligibility status impact the data sets used for state-level analysis of educational outcomes and economic mobility.

OAG provides legal counsel to state institutions and agencies regarding the interpretation and implementation of education laws, including residency requirements and constitutional considerations for undocumented students.

The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy and signs the annual state budget. The fiscal note indicates potential increases in general fund expenditures and aligns with the administration's broader policy goals regarding higher education access.

bill_summary: The Utility RELIEF Act implements comprehensive reforms to Maryland's energy utility regulations and programs to mitigate cost inflation for families. It transfers the Electric Universal Service Program to the Office of Home Energy Programs, establishes the Green and Renewable Energy Efficiency for Nonprofits Loan Program, and streamlines residential solar permitting. The bill modifies the EmPOWER Maryland program by excluding gas companies and reducing efficiency targets, restricts utility companies from recovering executive compensation and certain discretionary expenses through rates, and requires participation in regional transmission organizations. It also creates a registry for large load customers, such as data centers, and mandates a successor program to the current net energy metering system.
responsible_party: Public Service Commission, Maryland Energy Administration, Department of Human Services, and Department of Natural Resources
stakeholders: Residential and commercial utility customers, low-income households, nonprofit organizations, data center operators, and public service companies.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are significantly affected, most notably by $200,000,000 in contingent special fund appropriations from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) in FY 2027 ($100,000,000 for residential rate credits and $100,000,000 for renewable energy auctions). The bill also creates a mandated appropriation of unencumbered SEIF balances starting in FY 2028 and authorizes a $5,000,000 appropriation for the Green and Renewable Energy Efficiency for Nonprofits Loan Fund. State administrative expenditures increase by approximately $2,200,000 in FY 2027 for expanded staffing and consulting at the Public Service Commission, Office of People's Counsel, and other agencies. Local governments face mandates related to solar permitting and potential administrative costs for municipal utilities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directs the Governor to include specific appropriations in the annual budget (e.g., $100M for EmPOWER relief and SEIF balances). It also requires several reports to be submitted to the Governor regarding energy storage, net metering, and permitting streamlining.
The Comptroller is responsible for collecting the revenue from electric companies for the electric universal service program fund and placing it into the fund, which the bill reorganizes under OHEP.

The Treasurer serves on the Board of Public Works, which is granted specific authority by the bill to waive the 'termination for convenience' clause in multi-year renewable energy procurement contracts.

The bill specifically authorizes the Attorney General to seek judicial enforcement against any county or municipality that fails to comply with the new residential solar permitting and software requirements.

The bill reallocates the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) proceeds, which the fiscal note identifies as eliminating the current SEIF funding source for the Urban Trees Program administered by the Trust, necessitating $10M in general fund replacement.

The bill defines agricultural buildings for exemptions in building performance standards and excludes agricultural facilities from certain large load customer regulations. The Maryland Department of Agriculture is also notified of CPCN applications.
The bill includes mandated appropriations and significant special fund shifts that directly impact the state budget process and long-term fiscal planning managed by DBM.
The Department is consulted on the energy site-readiness initiative and is a recipient of notice for Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) applications for large energy projects.
The bill allocates a portion of SEIF clean energy proceeds to be used for school electrification and electric school bus deployment programs.

MDE is responsible for developing building energy performance standards, consulting on emissions targets, and analyzing the adequacy of energy plans in meeting state climate goals established by the bill.

DGS is authorized to issue RFPs for long-term leases for renewable energy projects and is involved in recommending the waiver of contract clauses for renewable energy procurements to the Board of Public Works.

DHCD is responsible for administering the low-income weatherization component of the electric universal service program and receives half of the fees collected from the large load customer registry for its energy efficiency programs.

The bill transfers the administration of the Electric Universal Service Program (EUSP) to the Office of Home Energy Programs (OHEP) within DHS, making it a primary implementing agency for energy assistance changes.

The Commissioner of Labor and Industry is required to determine prevailing wage rates for solar projects and large load facilities, and the Department is tasked with enforcing these wage requirements.

The Power Plant Research Program (PPRP) within DNR is tasked with a significant study on streamlined permitting, identifying priority energy sites, and reviewing CPCN applications for energy projects.
MDP is a recipient of notice for CPCN applications and coordinates with other agencies on the sustainable development initiatives impacted by the bill's energy policy changes.
The Maryland Aviation Administration (under MDOT) must determine if proposed transmission lines or generating stations pose hazards to aviation safety as part of the CPCN review process.

The bill establishes the 'Green and Renewable Energy Efficiency for Nonprofits Loan Program' (GREEN) within the Maryland Clean Energy Center to provide no-interest loans to nonprofits for energy efficiency and renewable systems.
MEA is a primary implementer, responsible for conducting alternative compliance fee auctions, managing the SEIF, providing renewable energy incentives, and coordinating multiple energy studies.
The bill explicitly states that the electric universal service program remains subject to audit by the Office of Legislative Audits.

As the consumer advocate, OPC is required to consult on annual rate reports, participate in the development of the net metering successor program, and sit in on major regulatory proceedings established by the bill.

The PSC is the primary regulator for most provisions of the bill, including utility rate setting, the large load customer registry, CPCN modifications, net metering transitions, and oversight of the EmPOWER Maryland program.
The Board is granted the authority to waive 'termination for convenience' clauses in state procurement contracts for renewable energy to help suppliers secure project financing.

bill_summary: This bill adds lead to the list of prohibited ingredients in cosmetic products and classifies violations as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act. It allows individuals to sue for civil damages and establishes the Harmful Hair Chemical Restitution Fund, administered by the Maryland Department of Health, to support research and treatment for conditions like uterine cancer and hair loss caused by harmful hair chemicals.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Consumers, cosmetic product manufacturers and retailers, and individuals suffering from health conditions caused by harmful hair chemicals.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by an estimated $540,793 in FY 2027, which includes $492,908 for enforcement by the Office of the Attorney General and $47,885 for administration by the Maryland Department of Health. General and special fund revenues increase minimally from penalties and interest, which are primarily directed to the newly established Harmful Hair Chemical Restitution Fund. Local governments are not significantly affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OAG's Division of Consumer Protection is a primary enforcer of the bill, as violations are classified as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices. The OAG is also co-responsible for developing a plan for the Harmful Hair Chemical Restitution Fund and is expected to see increased expenditures for enforcement staff.

MDH is the primary agency responsible for the public health regulations involved. It is authorized to investigate complaints, inspect premises, and collect samples. Additionally, MDH is tasked with administering the new Harmful Hair Chemical Restitution Fund and developing a plan for research and treatment in conjunction with the OAG.

DBM is the principal fiscal and personnel agency. The fiscal note indicates a need for additional staffing at both OAG and MDH to implement the bill, and the department will oversee the budget execution of the newly created special fund.

The bill establishes new civil liability for damages, including treble and punitive damages, and attorney's fees. The Judiciary will be responsible for adjudicating these civil actions brought by individuals for actual harm sustained.
As the state's chief financial agency, the Treasurer's Office will be responsible for the management and custody of the Harmful Hair Chemical Restitution Fund created by the bill.

The Comptroller acts as the state's chief financial officer and will likely be involved in the accounting and revenue collection processes related to the new restitution fund and its interest earnings.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies (MDH and OAG) responsible for implementing the bill and will receive the required plan and reports regarding the new fund.

bill_summary: The bill repeals the termination date for the mandated state funding for the University of Maryland Capital Region Medical Center (formerly the Prince George’s County Regional Medical Center), making an annual $10,000,000 appropriation permanent. It also updates the General Assembly's legislative findings regarding the facility's mission to transform healthcare delivery and address health disparities in Prince George’s County and the Southern Maryland region.
responsible_party: Governor and Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Residents of Prince George’s County and the Southern Maryland region, and the University of Maryland Medical System (UMMS)
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, general fund expenditures will increase by $10,000,000 annually beginning in fiscal year 2029, as the bill makes permanent a mandated appropriation that was previously scheduled to expire after fiscal year 2028. There is no impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that the Governor include a $10 million appropriation for the University of Maryland Capital Region Medical Center in the annual budget bill indefinitely, directly impacting the Governor's primary responsibility to propose the annual state budget.

As the principal agency for budget development and supervision of execution, DBM is responsible for incorporating this permanent $10 million mandated appropriation into the state's long-term fiscal planning and annual budget process.

The bill amends the Health – General Article of the Annotated Code of Maryland and concerns the funding and clinical viability of a major regional medical facility, falling under the Department's broader mission to oversee health policy and the state's health care system.

The HSCRC is responsible for ensuring the financial stability of Maryland hospitals and regulating their rates; the bill's findings specifically link the financial viability of the Capital Region Medical Center to these ongoing state operating grants.

The MHCC plans for the state's health system needs and works to improve access to care; the bill's objectives include growing access to high-quality clinical programs and addressing chronic health conditions in Prince George's County.

The medical center is a participating institution of the University of Maryland Medical System (UMMS), which is the state's largest academic medical system and maintains a strong institutional and clinical partnership with the University System of Maryland.

As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller is responsible for monitoring state revenues and paying state bills, including the mandated grants and operational funding preserved by this legislation.

The Treasurer's Office is responsible for the management and protection of state funds and acts as a key member of the Board of Public Works, which oversees significant state fiscal commitments such as the one made permanent by this bill.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Office of the Comptroller, in consultation with the Public Service Commission and PJM Interconnection, LLC, to conduct a study on the potential effects of exempting electricity used for specific agricultural purposes from the state sales and use tax. The study must include a fiscal impact estimate and be reported to the General Assembly by December 15, 2026. Agricultural purposes covered in the study include raising livestock or poultry, soil preparation and irrigation, and various activities related to seeds and crops.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Comptroller
stakeholders: Maryland farmers, livestock and poultry producers, electric utility companies, the Public Service Commission, and PJM Interconnection, LLC
fiscal_impact_summary: General fund expenditures for the Comptroller's Office may increase in fiscal 2027 to conduct the required study. The bill has no direct impact on state or local revenues as it mandates a report rather than an immediate change to tax law. Specific dollar estimates for the cost of the study are not provided in the fiscal note.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Office of the Comptroller to lead the study and report on the proposed sales and use tax exemption for electricity used for agricultural purposes.
The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to consult with the Public Service Commission, which regulates the electric companies required to provide usage and billing data for the study.

The subject matter of the study—electricity used for livestock, soil irrigation, and crop management—directly impacts the economic viability of the agricultural community that the department supports and regulates.

The bill is expected to increase general fund expenditures for the Comptroller's Office to conduct the study and involves long-term fiscal planning and revenue estimation related to the sales and use tax.
The proposed tax exemption would specifically benefit the agricultural and rural interests in Maryland's 18 rural counties that the council is tasked with advocating for and supporting.

As the administrative support for the Governor, the office oversees the executive branch agencies conducting the study and coordinates policy initiatives related to state taxation and agricultural support.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Comptroller and state agencies, which may be required to interpret existing tax laws and statutory definitions during the course of the study.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a Real Estate Advisory Committee within the Department of General Services to provide advice on commercial real estate trends, developments, and asset management best practices. It also expands reporting requirements for the Board of Public Works to the Legislative Policy Committee for high-value property acquisitions and long-term leases, and imposes community engagement requirements for the disposal of specific property in Baltimore City.
responsible_party: Department of General Services (DGS)
stakeholders: State agencies, the Maryland Board of Public Works, the commercial real estate sector, the Legislative Policy Committee, and community members in Baltimore City.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, general fund expenditures increase by $90,008 in FY 2027 to hire one administrative staff member to manage the advisory committee and handle expanded reporting requirements. Expenditures are projected to increase to $121,000 by FY 2031. There is no effect on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DGS is the primary implementing agency. The bill establishes the Real Estate Advisory Committee within DGS, requires DGS to provide staff, and mandates DGS to handle justifications and community engagement for property transactions.

The bill establishes new reporting and justification requirements for BPW regarding real estate acquisitions and leases, and restricts BPW from approving certain property sales without DGS community engagement.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller will be responsible for overseeing the new real estate approval and reporting requirements established by the bill.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the State Treasurer will be responsible for overseeing the new real estate approval and reporting requirements established by the bill.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new, permanent advisory body, the Real Estate Advisory Committee, which fits the definition of the commissions and committees categorized under this collective agency entity.

MDOT and its modal administrations (SHA, MTA, MPA, MAA) manage significant real estate and will be responsible for providing the required justifications and cost-benefit analyses for their relevant acquisitions and leases.
The fiscal note identifies USM as one of the agencies responsible for producing and disseminating the relevant required information for its property acquisitions and leases under the bill.
As a four-year institution of higher education, Morgan State is responsible for producing the required justifications and cost-benefit analyses for its real estate acquisitions and leases.
As a four-year institution of higher education, the college is responsible for providing the required justifications and cost-benefit analyses for its relevant real estate transactions.
The Real Estate Advisory Committee is required to submit annual findings and recommendations to the Governor, who also oversees the Department of General Services.
DBM is responsible for the state's personnel and budget execution; it will oversee the creation of the new staff position at DGS and the general fund expenditure associated with the bill.
